This study explores a coherent feedback control scheme within magnomechanics to enhance the entanglement shared among phonons, magnons, and photons. We detail the proposed feedback-based quantum protocol and demonstrate, through numerical analysis, that it consistently elevates the three-party correlation. Compared to a system lacking control, one employing our feedback control consistently achieves superior entanglement between the three components throughout nearly all timeframes.

This study introduces a comprehensive set of one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators $P_{a\rightarrow bc}^{\mu\{\nu\}\rho}$, where a particle of type $b$ splits into particles $b$ and $c$ embedded within a loop of type $a$. Defined within dimensional regularization for general dimensions $d = D - 2\epsilon$, the scalar coefficients associated with the resulting scalar tensor have been fully compiled for all 16 possible flavor transitions among quarks, antiquarks, and gluons. These results encompass cases involving fermion collinear splittings for the first instance. The presented work extends previous calculations by covering one-loop double-collinear operators for all flavors and gluons across any $d$ dimensions, as well as the newly derived triple-collinear matrix elements.

The process of applying the Characteristic 0 smooth desingularization technique, as developed by Abhyankar and Kunz during the 1960s and 70s, directly results in a negative result when most cases in the 1D local ring scenario under the Charactertic P setting are examined. In contrast, this paper demonstrates a "generalized version" of the Vistencis (1983) positive result, which specifically targets all the 1D G-rational local rings.

This study introduces the Suryakala-Nusantara project, dedicated to documenting sundials across the Indonesian archipelago. The initiative seeks to define the local concept of time, known locally as *suryakala*, which relies on the sun's movement for timekeeping. Although widely recognized in the West since antiquity, this concept is gaining attention from scholars studying the region. The project employs advanced digital techniques—including photogrammetry, computer vision, and machine learning—to digitally restore and preserve sundials. Additionally, the team has created computational algorithms that determine the precise time of day based on the shadows cast by these historical structures.

This study explores a future scenario where an Integrated Wireless Powering and Energy Harvesting (IRPEH) system supports Dual-Mode (D2D) system, all covered by an Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS). The primary goal is to maximize the sum rate of the IRNS-D2D system while ensuring a specific Rate-Per-Energy (RPE) threshold for users. To address this, an IRS configuration is proposed, which is optimized using a hybrid approach combining Semi-Orthogonal Successive Convex Decomposition (SOSCD) and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). Specifically, the DRL component is tasked with maximizing the IRNS-D2D sum rate, while the SOSCD method focuses on satisfying the RPE requirement. Notably, the DRL strategy operates without needing prior knowledge of channel statistics, distinguishing it from many traditional reinforcement learning approaches. Simulation results confirm that this joint optimization strategy significantly outperforms several baseline methods.

This study introduces a novel method for acquiring multi-point, distant controlled laser Doppler vibrometry (LDV) data using a single setup, facilitating the measurement of 2D surface vibrations. Validated through tests on a complex, heavily damped shell with diverse 2D vibration patterns, the method's accuracy was confirmed by comparing results against direct LDV scans using standard angular step sizes. Furthermore, the angular resolution for these multi-point, remotely guided LDV acquisitions was evaluated through comparisons using conventional scanning techniques.

We present an algorithmic solution to the isomorphism problem for first-order structures with binary relations, with a specific focus on spectra. In the course of solving this, a version of the canonical form for structures with dual relations is developed. This formulation serves as a direct extension of the established canonical forms applicable to linear structures. Additionally, a specific version of the canonical form is provided that is particularly suited for application in the context of the problem.

Although a programmable phase plate is typically employed to intentionally introduce contrast for enhancing image resolution in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEM), it may also be used to deliberately modify or remove existing phase aberrations. Utilizing a programmable phase disc with a 30-nm pitch amplitude aperture featuring a variable titanium nitride coating, this study successfully corrected various phase aberrations within a 200-kV TEM operating at an open source aperture condition. By systematically adjusting the effective phase shift across different zones, wavefront distortion was minimized, achieving a record-level improvement in wavefront transmissibility from an initial 0.013 to 0.007.

This study examines the impact of information leakage during the evaluation of a function $f$ on the computational resources required for its evaluation. We define the assessment complexity of a class $\mathcal{A}$ of functions on a set $X$ as the minimal complexity of an algorithm capable of evaluating every $f \in \mathcal{A}$ on any input $x \in X$. We demonstrate that assessment complexity is inherently tied to the underlying assessment costs. We introduce the concept of assessment costs as the evaluation complexity of an $f \in \mathcal{A}$ on inputs $x \in X$ that do not result in information leakage. We prove two primary results: first, assessment complexity equals the maximal assessment costs required; second, assessment costs are no greater than assessment complexity by a factor of two. These findings are generalized to scenarios where assessment costs are constrained to specific subsets of natural numbers. As an application, we introduce the notion of assessment costs within the real arithmetic model. We show that in this context, assessment costs correspond exactly to the assessment costs required for elementary functions, specifically those not inducing information leakage.

This study addresses the enumeration of distinct walk locations for specific numbers of steps within an $L_1$-norm sphere in $\mathbb{Z}^d$. The approach centers on deriving closed-form formulas that represent the number of walk configurations in such spheres, extending prior work by Holst (1989) who provided the enumeration for spherical spaces in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The methodology employed here draws upon a combinatorial framework previously utilized by the authors in studies of p-adic fields ($\mathbb{Q}_p$) and finite fields ($\mathbb{F}_p$) for $\mathbb{R}^d$-like structures in those non-Archimedean settings.

The expanded geometry associated with the Gambini-Olmedo-Pullin (GOP) spherically symmetric quantum gravity geometry, recently outlined in [arXiv:2103.01503], serves as the focus of our study. We examine both the structure and stability of the GOP expanded geometry while also calculating its quasinormal modes (QNMs). First, we detail the approach for determining these modes within GOP geometry, noting that their calculation had not previously been addressed. Subsequently, analyzing the impact varying the parameter $\lambda$ has on them, we find that this influence is negligible for $\lambda$ values small. Additionally, we compare the derived frequency to those from other recently proposed expanded geometries in GOP quantum gravity.

This study presents a first-principles investigation into the thermal shielding effects and specific heat capacity of the $\nu=0$ half-integer quantum Hall state in graphene superlattices subjected to magnetic fields. Our findings for the specific heat capacity align closely with existing experimental data. We also establish that the magnitude of thermal shielding is significantly influenced by both temperature and magnetic field strength, reaching its maximum at low temperatures and weak field conditions.

Conventional text-to-speech systems typically convert written characters into phonemes for speech generation. This paper introduces "MaskedDialogue," a novel framework that utilizes written dialogue as input to mask and restore specific segments during the generation phase to achieve context-aware speech synthesis. The model operates through a multi-task learning strategy comprising a speech generation network and a written dialogue prediction network. During training, this setup ensures the generator maintains a strong understanding of textual dialogue through continuous prediction tasks. The system effectively leverages rich semantic and pragmatic information contained in dialogue scripts to produce more coherent and natural speech. The model was trained using Google's public ConversationalPhoneDialogues dataset and assessed against the Microsoft DialogueSynthesis challenge dataset for comparative analysis. Experimental results demonstrate that, particularly in single-turn conversations, the framework significantly outperforms traditional text-based approaches by exploiting the advantages of text-input generation.

Imitation learning represents a prominent strategy for robot skill transfer, yet current methods often fail to generalize effectively when faced with variations in observation or measurement noise. We introduce a new framework called HSP-PRe (Hidden Space Projection Predicitive Reasoning) that combines domain knowledge from physics and chemistry with a predictive reasoning approach to robustly extract and align semantically relevant observations across domains. This method leverages generative modeling to predict missing observations based on learned environmental knowledge, thereby enabling the reasoning process necessary for reliable inter-domain skill adaptation. Experiments conducted on two complex, multi-step robotic tasks demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms existing imitation learning techniques in successfully transferring skills between disparate observation spaces.

While adversarial examples have been established as a significant vulnerability for deep learning classifiers, their impact on generative models remains poorly understood. This paper introduces "Malicious Generative Frameworks" (MGFs), which include two specific attack strategies: MGF Injection and MGF Evasion. MGF Injection allows an attacker to insert designated target data points into the probability density function (PDF) of a generative model via injection data, causing the model to produce outputs heavily concentrated around these targets. Conversely, MGF Evasion enables the removal of selected member data from the PDF of an existing MGF. We outline attack methodologies applicable to both dense and sparse data environments for these two frameworks and detail attack algorithms designed to achieve their respective goals. Testing on two real-world datasets demonstrates significant performance gains for both attacks. Additionally, we investigate countermeasures designed to mitigate these risks.

Climate alteration conspiracy theories have become increasingly widespread in recent times, often gaining traction in various online spaces. This study examines the specific online platforms where these narratives are most prevalent and analyzes the platforms' structural characteristics that facilitate the dissemination of such misinformation. By scraping Twitter and Reddit to locate and differentiate between conspiracy and non-conspiracy accounts, along with gathering data from Wikipedia and YouTube, the researchers identified the unique ecosystem supporting these claims. The analysis reveals a fragmented platform structure characterized by insularity, a lack of cross-over, and an abundance of self-referential content. These findings suggest that the online environment promoting climate conspiracy content operates within an "echo chamber," where users are submerged in a constant stream of reinforcing information without exposure to contrasting viewpoints.

The D0 experiment's LHC analyzed a dataset from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, accumulating an integrated luminosity of 137 fb$^{-1}$. This study examines a search for shadow matter occurring in single top events, alongside events involving two top quarks. The sample was scrutinized within the dileptonic, leptonic, and quark decay channels, utilizing the latter to constrain background rates. The observed event counts align with Standard Model predictions, leading to limits on specific beyond-Standard Model processes. Specifically, the coupling strength between a heavy vector boson ($Z'$) and the electroweak current is restricted to |gV| < 0.022 (95% C.L.) in the quark-lepton channel, whereas the quark-only mode provides a limit of |gV| < 0.020. The study also establishes limits on anomalous quartic gauge couplings in the quark-only mode: |C1γ| < 1.1×10$^{-3}$ and |C1W| < 1.0×10$^{-3}$ (95% C.L.).

The evaluation of high-luminosity $J/\psi$ production sites is a priority for the Chinese community, as such facilities could yield up to $10^{12}$ $J/\psi$ particles annually. These dense sources offer a unique opportunity to generate vast quantities of antineutrons and hyperons, enabling the design of specialized beam lines for future projects. This feasibility study estimates the potential yields and corresponding fluxes of these particles at energies around 5–7 GeV, demonstrating that current beam line technologies are sufficient to direct them into next-generation accelerator facilities as focused beams. By leveraging this significant flow, researchers can achieve unprecedented beam intensities and explore novel methodologies to investigate the properties of free antineutrons and hyperons.

We have developed 3D hydrodynamic simulations to examine how accretion rates within protoplanetary systems influenced by a hierarchical triple star configuration are modified. By comparing these results with standard models that feature co-rotating binaries, we found that while the binary accretion rate is typically 2–3 times greater than that of a singleton star, triple systems exhibit a split behavior: the inner star's accretion is enhanced by a factor of ~10, whereas the outer star sees a suppression to roughly half a solar rate. Consequently, total accretion in these triples is approximately 30 times higher than in single-star cases. We attribute this mechanism to efficient angular momentum transfer via the dense gas in the intervening disc, which rapidly depletes the inner star's circumstellar material. Finally, we assessed the impact of this triple-star formation channel on the standard initial mass function (IMF) and its resulting stellar birth rates.

We explore inherently flat Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) models defined within a lattice framework. In this approach, inherent flatness signifies a termination of FLRW expansion at specific radii beyond which geodesic paths cannot continue, creating an outer boundary for the universe. This scenario is examined in both three and two spatial dimensions, with an emphasis on physical constants regarding speed and travel times. Spatially, the three-dimensional topology follows that of $\mathbb{R}^2 \times S^1$, exhibiting a singular cusp at its outer boundary, while the two-dimensional case mirrors the metric of a cone with its tip sealed off. Although matter dynamics within such a bounded outer region face significant challenges, the article contends that this topology induces an effective cosmic barrier. This mechanism mimics a singular inner core of the universe, allowing the system to serve as a viable alternative to standard black hole formulations.

Image partitioning is a fundamental computer vision task with broad applications in segmentation, denoising, and other related fields. In this paper, we introduce a new probabilistic model that utilizes image partitioning results and couples them with the reconstruction process. Unlike many existing approaches, our proposed method requires no manual parameter tuning and demands neither pre-convergence of the reconstruction algorithm nor prior denoising steps. We have implemented the model on various numerical networks, including a fully conjugate gradient algorithm that guarantees semi-convergence essential for effective denoising performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art partitioning techniques across various metrics.

The measurement of spin parameters for supermassive black holes (BHs) offers a promising avenue for detecting ultralight bosonic fields, which may serve as viable dark matter candidates. When spinning up, a massive BH can serve as a reservoir, allowing a surrounding cloud of these hypothetical bosons to extract energy and angular momentum through the mechanism of superradiance, thereby altering the BH's spin. Consequently, spin evolution constitutes a critical observational indicator. This study utilizes the complete sample from the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration to analyze the relationship between spin and the mass of these bosons. By focusing on the EHT population, we achieve superior sensitivity to deviations in spin evolution compared to previous investigations. Our findings indicate that, assuming axially symmetric boson clouds, the EHT sample allows us to constrain the mass of these bosons to the range $m_{\Phi} \in [10^{-13}, 10^{-10}] \, \mathrm{GeV}/c^2$ for spin magnitudes below 0.9, a limit that extends to $m_{\Phi} \in [10^{-12}, 10^{-9.5}] \, \mathrm{GeV}/c^2}$ for spins between 0.5 and 0.9. Furthermore, we evaluate the potential of future observational campaigns, demonstrating that a dataset comprising 100 quasar spins could tighten these bounds by a factor of

High-fidelity software simulators for spiking neural network (SNN) applications are essential for validating SNN algorithms and evaluating their suitability for implementation on neuromorphic hardware. This paper introduces "brian2Loihi," an emulator of Intel's Loihi neuromorphic processor constructed upon the Brian 2 neural network simulation framework. This tool enables the rapid prototyping of Loihi applications by allowing seamless switching between software emulation and hardware execution. The implementation adheres closely to Loihi's architectural specifications, accurately reflecting its neuron and spike synapse models, as well as its specific constraint limits. This adherence was verified through a rigorous comparison of simulated versus hardware outcomes across various benchmark circuits. Additionally, the brian2Loihi emulator supports standard optimization strategies, such as reducing the number of neurons and minimizing synaptic counts to lower overall network size.

Accurately diagnosing magnetic field structures is essential for understanding solar eruptions. This study utilizes 15-minute observations of a microflare to explore the concurrent evolution of magnetic field parameters. We tracked storm center locations and measured both duration and radio emission intensity across the radio spectrum (15 MHz to 300 MHz). The results indicate a strong correlation among these variables, suggesting they all trace the state of the underlying magnetic field. Specifically, as storm duration shortens, the radio burst becomes more intense. This suggests that smaller-scale, shorter-duration storms are driven by more vigorous flaring energy release, likely pointing to more dynamic magnetic reconnection processes.

Atom-based sensors utilizing optical traps have shown significant promise for detecting magnetic and electric fields. However, current experimental methods rely on complex setups combining optical tweezers and magneto/optic traps positioned within high-power magnetic shielding, creating a barrier for widespread adoption. To address this, we introduce a simplified solution by integrating the trap directly onto a chip using on-chip optical fibers. Our eight-stage fabrication process yields a compact device measuring 10 mm × 15 mm × 0.5 mm. This micro-fabricated atomic apparatus successfully creates a magnetic field of 10 G across an atomic optical sheet spanning 100 μm × 1000 μm, sufficient to confine Rubidium atoms. We anticipate that this system will facilitate the development of chip-scale atomic sensing and computing technologies.

This study examines stationary accretion flows of a black hole derived from the 1D symmetric subset of the Vlasov system, where particles originate from a sphere with finite radius $R$ and non-zero momentum. We determine the unique flow configuration for any specified sphere size $R$ and momentum distribution, analyzing how this initial state influences the resulting dynamics. Our findings reveal that increasing particle momentum amplifies the asymptotic infall velocity at the event horizon and enhances the magnitude of the flow's enthalpy. Geometrically, the flow structure shifts from a single cell to a multi-cell configuration as the sphere's radius $R$ grows. Furthermore, we outline the precise mathematical requirements on $R$ and momentum that dictate whether the fluid reaches a singular state of infinite density at the horizon. These theoretical results are compared against numerical simulations performed by others, demonstrating strong agreement.

We investigate the spontaneous emission of a pointlike dipolar atom situated near a slender, perfectly conducting mirror. Our results demonstrate that the mirror's confinement geometry can drastically alter an atom's transport dynamics and radiation properties based on its position. Specifically, when the dipole's orientation is parallel, the dipole's center of mass experiences strong binding toward the mirror, whereas perpendicular orientation yields weak confinement. Furthermore, the mirror influences radiation properties based on its dimensions relative to the dipole. For a sub-wavelength slit, spontaneous emission rates are primarily dictated by the dipole's distance from the surface; conversely, in the limit of a wide flared opening, emission rates depend solely on the mirror's geometric shape rather than proximity.

The newly formed Westerlund 2 cluster, situated approximately 10 kiloparsecs from the Sun, is a significant young stellar object. In this study, we analyzed 1,020 stars within the cluster and its immediate surroundings using the HST/STROPHOTO instrument. Our analysis reveals that the mass function (MF) in this region is continuous, showing no evidence of a low-mass turn-over typically associated with initial mass function studies. The distribution of stellar masses is well-modeled by a standard Salpeter MF, with a slope of -2.35. The majority of these stars are giants, likely evolved from members of the same initial population as the current W2-1 cluster members. The radius of the study area is approximately 1.5 parsecs, which is roughly 1,500 AU in radius. This study examines a specific type of nonlocal, fourth-order Choquard equation featuring variable exponents and involving combined subcritical and critical standard growth conditions. The authors develop ground state solutions representing exponentially decaying waves, utilizing Moser iteration to establish uniform bounds for first and second derivatives, a procedure requiring intricate estimation, and applying the "linking" approach from critical variable exponent theory. These contributions generalize prior work by Ruf-Taggart and others to this more complex nonlocal setting, yielding standardized biharmonic Choquard equations. The research also provides the capability to analyze the equation's behavior under the expansion of the parameter \(\lambda\), thereby identifying a threshold value beyond which no solution exists.

Handwritten document images (HDIs) suffer from artifacts like noise, uneven lighting, and textual deformations that typically impair their performance on tasks such as handwritten recognition. To address this, we introduce HDI enhancement as a specific discipline aimed at automating the correction of such defects. Drawing inspiration from successful applications in other areas, we developed a generative model to refine HDIs through a proposed architecture, Multi-task Adversarial Network for HDI enhancement (MAN-Net). This network introduces two key components: a shape restoration network designed to correct deformations, and an illumination normalization network to handle lighting variations. Moreover, an additional recognition task is integrated as a supervisory mechanism to better guide the generative process. Extensive testing demonstrates that MAN-Net significantly outperforms current methods, enhancing HDIs and subsequently boosting overall handwritten recognition accuracy.

Recent years have seen significant advancements in Information Technology, particularly within the domains of software development and hardware capabilities, sparking a global surge in the adoption of technology for various purposes. Among these applications, Character Extraction (OE) stands out as a critical tool for digitizing physical documents into text format. Historically, this process relied heavily on Manual Entry Technology (MET), a method prone to errors due to its labor-intensive nature. In contrast, Character Extraction (OE) leverages Intelligent Systems to enhance the speed, accuracy, and reliability of this digitization process. This study evaluates current Optic Character Recognition (OCR) frameworks by conducting a comparative analysis of various OCR sources to identify the most suitable option. Furthermore, the research incorporates Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to refine extraction outcomes. The proposed methodology utilizes Intel's One Vision API for image data access, Microsoft Azure Services for extracting key-value pairs, and Microsoft Azure Translater for language conversion. Validated through real-world samples of common Indonesian identification documents—including the Kartu Tanda Penduduk ( KTP ) and Kartu Keluarga ( KK )—the results indicate that combining OCR with NLP analysis yields superior performance compared to using OCR independently.

In the context of IEEE 802.11p standard vehicle communications, data transmission occurs through an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) environment augmented with unmodeled, time-varying nonlinear distortions. This research examines the nonlinear characteristics of the dual-hop channel, specifically focusing on how noise propagates through it. The study also evaluates the channel's nonlinearity by analyzing its response to input signals of differing power levels. Addressing these distortions, the paper proposes implementing a channel estimation technique that utilizes time-smoothing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks. The proposed method was validated through computer simulations, demonstrating performance that surpasses both the conventional Least Mean Square (LMS) algorithm and an existing linear Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) variant within the paper.

Picture colorization has long been recognized as a fundamental challenge in computer vision, particularly relevant to astronomy, since many prominent objects in astronomical images are faint or obscured by bright hydrogen emission lines from nebulae, which appear red. Historically, scientists have used filters to isolate specific wavelengths, but the resulting monochrome output limits their ability to perceive certain objects. Introducing color could help scientists visualize these data more effectively, a goal increasingly supported by deep learning methods. This study introduces an advanced colorization framework that utilizes Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate synthetic colored versions of astronomical picture, demonstrating superior visual quality and structural coherence compared to traditional unsupervised and supervised deep learning alternatives.

This study introduces the methodology for constructing a finite set of linear neural networks with independent random weights and biases (pulsed uniform distribution) aimed at minimizing the loss function defined by $\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(y(n)-\sum_{j=1}^{M}b(j)g\left(\sum_{i=1}^{C}a(i)n+c(i)\right)\right)^{2}$, where the non-linear activation function $g$ is the logistic function. The optimization of the parameters $b(j)$ and $c(i)$ is performed using the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm. The theoretical framework also provides a bound on the required network size $K$ as a function of the inputs. The proposed structure is validated through its ability to approximate both the XOR logic gate and the bivariate function $y = f(x_1,x_2) = x_1^2 + 2x_1x_2 + x_2^2 + 2x_1 + 2x_2 + 1$.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECFERC) was established in 2021 to provide a platform for early-careil researchers (ECR) involved in the European Climate Change Alliance (ECCLA). ECRs constitute a pivotal segment of the climate research community, and the committee's primary objective is to ensure their specific needs and concerns are articulated and addressed. Since its inception, the ECFERC has been dedicated to identifying opportunities for European climate researchers. This document details the committee's formation, including its membership composition and the strategic framework guiding its activities throughout the 2021 -- 2022 period.

We introduce a novel method for generating line waves at wavelengths spanning visible to infrared light by employing dual metastructures. In this setup, two distinct unit cells are placed in close proximity within a single metallic substrate backed by dielectric layers. By tuning the dual resonators, we create two closely spaced resonant peaks that induce strong dispersion, allowing the resulting phase variation to support wave propagation confined to a narrow strip. This mechanism, grounded in near-resonant high dispersion, enables the generation of line waves guided by the dual metastructure.

Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) represents a pivotal area within cognitive robotics, aiming to equip robots with decision-making and reasoning capabilities to perform complex tasks effectively. A significant challenge lies in creating accessible systems where end-users can easily build cognitive models based on their specific knowledge of a task. Furthermore, these systems must support seamless integration of new information, such as updated user preferences or altered task dynamics. This study presents an open-source, extensible framework designed to facilitate HRC problem formulation and data analysis by unifying state-of-the-art methods. Built upon a production-level software architecture, this framework accommodates multiple machine and reinforcement learning approaches for analyzing collaborative behaviors. By leveraging this system, we demonstrate how to model binary-coded physical interactions between people and robots using both machine and reinforcement learning techniques. Additionally, the framework allows for updating task models with fresh data to incorporate additional binary features or features with additional states. Finally, we enhance these task models by integrating information about environmental changes, specifically the addition of new objects to the task.

A naive approach to estimating conditional medians using quantile regression often suffers from bias, a flaw that negatively impacts downstream applications like the calculation of the Mean Absolute Deviation Around the Median (ADDM). This paper introduces a modified, nonparametric quantile regression estimator that mitigates this bias without incurring additional computational costs. Valid statistical inference for the bias-corrected 3-MADAM metric is provided through the use of block bootstrap methods. The proposed methodology is validated via simulations and an actual case study featuring Minotaur's rotating magnetosphere.

Extraction of relations from textual data stands as a pivotal natural language processing challenge, with applications in extracting schema elements from wiki articles for knowledge curation and constructing structured knowledge graphs. However, achieving top-tier performance necessitates extensive labeled training data, which is scarce. This research addresses these constraints by integrating external knowledge graphs to enhance the training of sequence models. Specifically, we enhance training with pre-computed entity pair disambiguation scores. Empirical results demonstrate an improvement of 2.5% in F1 scores for a standalone text model and a gain of 22.0% for a co-trained pair, highlighting the training knowledge graph's substantial impact on sequence model learning.

The yield of quarkonia formed through fragmentation in a momentum-anisotropic, $\tau^d$-expanding medium (for $d=3, 4, \dots, n$) is investigated under extreme QCD conditions defined by both temperature and chemical potential. The in-medium Debye mass is derived as a function of the anisotropic variables to evaluate quarkonium production via the fragmentation of free and charm quarks. The calculations employ thermal phase space integrals within an anisotropic environment and utilize the exact anisotropic finite-temperature, finite chemical potential quark-antiquark potential in the real part to assess the yield. The results are presented in the context of high-energy collisions, specifically focusing on LHC and heavy-ion environments.

The rare-earth ruthenate Tb$_3$RuO$_7$ exhibits a magnetic transition at 0.6 K, characterized by a sharp peak in specific heat and a bifurcation of magnetic susceptibility. A detailed analysis of low-temperature AC susceptibility and NMR data reveals that the system's ground state comprises two distinct components: an antiferromagnetic (AFM) portion involving ferromagnetic (FM) chains of alternating spin-3/2 Ru segments, and a thermally persistent disordered fraction. The AFM portion is driven by interchain interactions, which are modulated by the system in a field due to the presence of FM segments. This non-uniform internal magnetic field is responsible for the observed disorder. Theoretical modeling utilizing a spin-3/2 Hamiltonian, incorporating both single-ion anisotropy and interchain exchange, successfully reproduces the experimental findings. The study concludes that the ground state of Tb$_3$RuO$_7$ is a complex mixture of competing AFM and FM interactions among Ising-like spin-3/2 Ru chains, a behavior analogous to that seen in spin-5/2 U Ru$_3$O$_7$.

Training deep neural networks typically demands extensive data; however, acquiring reliable labels for certain data types, such as video and audio, remains costly and difficult. Model distillation offers a viable solution by leveraging a robust pre-trained model to guide the training of a simpler network on limited specialized datasets. This strategy is particularly effective when combining models across different modalities. Although distillation facilitates such transfers, existing methods often yield students with poor temporal consistency and robustness, thereby restricting their utility in time-series forecasting. This paper introduces two innovations to enhance time-aware distillation. Initially, we identify and analyze issues in current approaches that impair the student's capacity to learn temporal dynamics. Subsequently, we propose Modulated Recurrent Attention (MRA), an innovative feedback mechanism designed to inject strong inherent temporal structures into the hidden states of the distilled model. Empirical results demonstrate that our student models achieve robust functional equivalence to their teachers while exhibiting superior temporal learning capabilities.

Machine learning models often struggle when applied to new data distributions distinct from their training sets, a problem frequently rooted in covariate shift. To address this, researchers have explored two main avenues: transfer learning and domain adaptation. However, these methods typically require assumptions about invariant attributes across domains or knowledge of shifting features, which is often unrealistic in practical scenarios. In contrast, this work introduces semi-generative modeling—a framework designed for settings where domain-specific information is unavailable. Using a cause-effect framework, this approach utilizes semi-generative training data alongside general test inputs to produce a robust predictor. Specifically, it restructures the input space into causal components, performs domain alignment within these structures, and constructs the final model. The methodology is applicable to both supervised and unsupervised tasks, offering theoretical guarantees for covariate shift correction in both cases. Empirical evaluations on synthetic datasets and real-world datasets confirm that these results surpass existing state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/jeffkang95/semi-generative-modeling.

Deep learning serves as a leading approach for solving machine learning challenges, yet its operational mechanisms remain elusive. This difficulty stems from the fact that these models consist of vast ensembles of algebraic equations which, existing within an immense solution space, admit numerous valid configurations capable of performing effectively. Among these variables, the geometrical characteristics of the underlying data exert a decisive influence on model success. This book illuminates how the functional outcomes of deep learning are fundamentally rooted in the underlying geometry, a perspective intended to clarify the model's internal workings and potentially streamline both their design and optimization.

We demonstrate that within the context of main effects, interactions contribute to grid grid minima. These occur when the function's oscillations along individual primary variables are approximated by holding other variables constant at specific levels. By allowing these fixed levels to vary, the concept of an additive model emerges as the foundation. Consequently, both the model and its associated grid minima are approximations whose accuracy hinges on the variables' values. This discussion highlights that the concept of grid minima is not isolated but rather integral to the broader framework of main effects and interactions in general.

Deep learning models are increasingly central to identifying jets within the LHC environment, as these objects represent the dominant component in hadronic particle collisions. This study applies Layerwise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to a quark-gluon jet classifier constructed from hadronic variables, aiming to enhance the interpretability of its internal decision logic. The analysis indicates that this deep neural network utilizes information consistent with established jet physics findings. Specifically, it shows sensitivity to the momentum distributions of charged and neutral particles, as well as the spatial and momentum substructure.

In this study, we introduce two new families of numbers r-Stirling of the first and second kind called under degenerate conditions. For the second type (when r is smaller than or equal to d), we show an equivalence between Degenerate r-Stirling numbers of the second kind and a newly formed variation of the Entringer relation. Additionally, we derive a set of attributes for these numbers, including their entry for a poincare-polynomial and Derivative relations, and display an ultrametric property within the associated Degenerate Stirling Polynomials. Finally, we show how to apply this new family to partitions of the type being considered and to random variable theory, specifically their mean and variance.

We demonstrate that every representation defined on an algebra of set functions—specific ordinary, gray, or configured around dual set organzations inheriting symmetry from subsets of an arbitrary finite group $G$—can be constructed exclusively through combinations of certain fundamental symmetric representations. These building-block functions are notably either irreducible or isomorphic to one another.

We examine Weyl manifolds (M,g) featuring a Killing vector field X for which every path remaining sub-invariant under X constitutes a geodesic. In this specific context, our analysis reveals X functions as a geodesic vector field, and furthermore, the manifold (M,g) adheres to the conditions of being Weyl-conformal to a Riemannian manifold where the signature differs.

Diffusion probabilistic models have recently achieved major success in supercomputing-scale applications, such as denoising particulate systems. In the context of Fermi-Dirac ensembles, these models typically generate complex negative diffusion coefficients that result in significant Monte Carlo integration challenges known as "phase cancellation" or the "Hubbard sign problem." To combat this, we introduce an improved denoising strategy that utilizes these models to target only the diffusion rate's absolute magnitude (the real, positive denominator), effectively resolving the Hubbard sign issue. Furthermore, we replace traditional neural architectures with complex-valued networks capable of computing complex outputs required for full variable estimation. This integrated approach yields enhanced accuracy and computational efficiency across diverse many-body test cases, marking a notable advancement in applying machine learning to statistical physics.

In this framework, the observed Higgs boson emerges as the lighter state from a Nambu-Goldstone-Bostone (NGC) pair that forms following the reduction of this symmetry. Perceptual shifts within immersive virtual reality environments manifest in diverse ways, including modifications to vision, hearing, and other sensory modalities. This review examines current literature alongside emerging theoretical frameworks to explore the underlying mechanisms driving these changes. Going forward, shadow aspects—subtle or overlooked elements of these alterations—are explored in detail. Such scrutiny serves a functional purpose: enhancing our general understanding of how senses work by revealing the full scope of virtual manipulations, thereby aiding the development of better safety protocols and guidelines for VR users.

> We introduce an adaptation of BigScience's multilingual model generation framework to support five additional languages: Arabic, Chinese, Korean, and two others. To achieve this, we trained distinct, language-specific GPT-2 and GPT-3 architectures. Our study also examines how the model handles generated text in these new languages and addresses the challenges of integrating data from each.

This study examines the statistical likelihood of creating binary systems with specific masses through the fragmentation of a spinning progenitor core under varying conditions. The analysis relies on statistical equilibrium principles and conservation of total angular momentum. Key variables explored include the parent core's mass ($M_{parent}$) and its spin parameter ($\alpha_{parent}$), as the resulting mass distribution of the binary's components is a function of these values. The work first outlines the theoretical framework and previously derived mass probability density functions for various combinations of $M_{parent}$ and $\alpha_{parent}$. It then calculates the associated median masses for the resulting binaries across the same parameter space. Finally, the resulting mass median values are compared against observations from gravitational wave detectors to assess their consistency with actual astrophysical events.

This method addresses computational inefficiencies associated with traditional ICA by arming it with additional features. Specifically, the approach integrates optimization strategies derived from metaheuristic techniques alongside specific feature enhancements. We reintroduce a variation of choiceless time complexity to analyze first-order logic with bounded quantifier depth. Distinguishing specific structures relative to this variation provides logictyping results equivalent to those obtained using bounded leaf-sensitive quasi-quantifier (LQP) with structure and map counting. As a direct application, we offer a simplified demonstration linking LQP with bounded true cardinality to bounded true cardinality. Distinguishing structures relative to LQP with bounded leaf-sensitive capabilities yields depth lower bounds for both bounded LQP and the limited extended polynomial calculus. For instance, applying this method offers a streamlined proof that elementary time cannot compactly reduce to PTime via polynomial calculus.

An open domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^{n}$ is termed $\sigma$-elementary (with $\sigma = 2k + 1$ being odd) when there exists an analytic polynomial map $p: C^n \to C^{k}$ and an analytic polynomial $q: C^n \to C$ such that $\Omega = p^{-1}(D) \cap p^{\sim 1}(-\infty, 0)$, where $D \subset C^{k}$ is a bounded open subset. In this paper, we present novel examples of such domains for every dimension $n$ and order $\sigma$.

Assertion-driven verification is a key component of the formal validation community, yet existing approaches often fail to handle complex assertions effectively. This challenge is largely due to the difficulty in determining the truth value of compound structures, such as nested temporal logic, without a proper framework. This paper introduces the "Explain for Framework" (Xfpf), designed to validate such intricate conditions by first decomposing them into elementary clauses and then assessing each individually. The system was implemented and tested against synthetic examples as well as real-world industrial challenges. Testing demonstrated that Xfpf successfully identifies all verification targets, handles design specifications containing nested temporal logic, and operates efficiently.

Traffic incidents significantly disrupt traffic flow and elevate operational costs, making rapid detection a critical area of study for both current and future Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS). While researchers have explored using real-time traffic data and historical patterns for incident identification, few have explored the potential of geosocial networks. This study investigates Twitter data geotagged within the New York City metropolitan area to develop a method for pinpointing incidents. The proposed approach hinges on identifying and analyzing the temporal and spatial relationships among spatio-temporal words found in Twitter posts. Specifically, incident detection is achieved by locating empty spatio-temporal words, defined as words whose predicted time or position based on the model lacks actual data. Furthermore, to mitigate biases toward popular landmarks, we introduce a weighting mechanism that adjusts for landmark popularity and user travel routines. Empirical results indicate that our model outperforms baseline methods, achieving an accuracy of 84.62% in identifying incident locations and 74.34% in timing.

Cross-correlating CMB anisotropies with large-scale structure (LSS) offers a highly sensitive technique for probing primordial non-Gaussianity, serving as an independent and valuable complement to CMB polarization studies. As upcoming surveys advance, sensitivity will increase significantly, making the estimation of higher-order cross-correlation statistics like the bispectrum essential. This paper introduces a swift method for generating mock bispectra based on established transfer functions and power spectra. By utilizing Gaussian realizations and applying baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) and redshift-space distortion (RSD) corrections, this approach produces robust estimates of the true bispectrum. Validated against N-body simulations of $\Lambda\Lambda$CDM models covering various redshifts, survey volumes, and observation modes, the proposed methodology yields accurate results with minimal computational expense. Its exceptional speed renders it particularly suitable for survey planning phases, where extensive survey configurations require quick, approximate bispectrum evaluations.

This paper introduces a probabilistic programming model designed to infer the accuracy of neural network classifiers, specifically when only a subset of the test dataset is annotated. By integrating deep generative models with Bayesian inference, we utilize a likelihood function grounded in the margin aliasing phenomenon to regulate accuracy estimates. This mechanism ensures that derived parameters are compatible with observable model outputs on a batch of test images, of which some are labeled and others remain unlabeled. Because our method relies on the margin aliasing principle, labeled data serves as a verifiable proxy for accuracy, allowing us to evaluate how well specific accuracy estimates generalize to the unlabeled portion of the dataset. Furthermore, our framework enables the inference of auxiliary metrics, such as class-specific error rates and data augmentation impact. We also present enhanced algorithms for estimating accuracy that accelerate inference by orders of magnitude compared to established variational approaches.

Online rumors have become increasingly prevalent in China, particularly within the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. The study's primary objective is to analyze the mechanisms behind the dissemination of these online falsehoods and their subsequent impact. To achieve this, the researchers constructed an original dissemination model and evaluated its fitting accuracy. The model's parameters were estimated using maximum likelihood methodology, while the distribution of online rumors was analyzed through minimum entropy methods. The findings indicate that the proposed mechanism effectively captures the dissemination dynamics of online rumors in China. Furthermore, the results reveal that online rumors exhibit a left-skewed distribution. The implications of these discoveries are discussed in relation to their strategic value in combating the spread of misinformation and online rumors in China.

This paper examines the effects of reducing dimensionality on the classification accuracy of hyperspectral imagery, with a specific case study focused on the hyperspectral pixel classification task. Dimensionality reduction is essential for managing the excessive data volume inherent in hyperspectral imagery; however, this process can inadvertently obscure significant information, thereby potentially degrading final classification accuracy. Our investigation addresses a critical research question: does dimensionality reduction invariably impair accuracy, or can it sometimes enhance it? Through comprehensive empirical analysis, we determine that dimensionality reduction does not consistently degrade results and can, in specific scenarios, improve them. Additionally, we evaluate various reduction techniques, revealing that different methods yield disparate impacts on accuracy depending on the data.

Recent research has shown that neural network models for natural language processing often exhibit irrelevance in the context of training data, meaning they only activate on task-rank language. This paper builds upon the reduction method introduced by Franck et al. (2021), demonstrating its applicability to state-of-the-art off-the-shelf sequence transduction systems. Our findings indicate that trained models reduce to a compact, dense layer sensitive solely to non-padded tokens within the head position, with all other vocabulary tokens effectively becoming irrelevant. This computational process scales linearly with sequence length and preserves performance. Furthermore, the study outlines the conditions under which such reduction occurs and introduces "VocabDrop," a novel regularization technique. Vocablow encourages weights associated with unused vocabulary to approach zero and strengthens the irrelevance of components not utilized during transduction. Finally, the paper describes "VowkMM," a weight mask mechanism capable of distilling trained models into sparse, length-independent forms without compromising task accuracy.

Determining the 3D structures of proteins is essential for understanding their biological functions. While NMR provides experimental data like chemical shifts that are typically used to validate protein conformations in solution, these measurements are prone to noise. To enhance both the validity and predictive accuracy of protein structures, a new approach is proposed that utilizes high-level quantum mechanical calculations to determine accurate amide proton chemical shifts. Specifically, a multi-step quantum framework was developed: it first applies the Gaussian-2 program to optimize nitrogen atom geometries within peptide bonds, and then employs the Gaudi-1 program to calculate the resulting amide proton chemical shifts. This highly accurate, two-step optimization strategy allows for the efficient and precise prediction of proton shifts, even when the electronic anisotropy of neighboring groups is considered.

Loss function selection is critical in deep learning model development, yet modifying them for specific tasks or data remains a frequent necessity. This study investigates a common approach to optimizing modified losses: re-estimating the parameters of the base loss via cross-validation within every gradient step. We demonstrate that this technique yields superior performance compared to standard methods like empirical risk minimization (ERM) updated solely by historical batch data. Furthermore, we introduce Regret Analysis, a novel framework grounded in online learning theory, to examine this methodology. Unlike previous studies, our analysis provides the first bounds specifically accounting for the simultaneous modification of both the learning algorithm and the loss function. The effectiveness of this lsso modification strategy, along with our proposed method, is validated on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

The primary objective of this work is to examine the parquet equation within the framework of Green's functions, utilizing a diagrammatic approach grounded in Hamiltonian considerations. Within this theory, four distinct interaction vertices are defined: the single-particle, many-particle, and two kinds of parquet vertices. These vertices are linked through specific diagrammatic rules that adhere to strict symmetry constraints, ensuring all particle species are treated equally. By analyzing the interaction and Green's functions in terms of these parquet vertices and their associated diagrams, this theory offers a fresh perspective that could help resolve the single-particle vertex determination problem. Ultimately, this research aims to avert double-counting of interactions and facilitate the calculation of multi-particle interactions from fundamental, first-principles data.

The technique of exciton Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) offers a promising avenue for achieving superconductivity within the framework of non-zero temperature non-BCS superconductors. In this study, we employ an $\textbf{ab~initio}$ approach to investigate the formation of exciton polaritons in non-superconducting $\textbf{TiSe}_2$. Our findings reveal that non-superconducting $\textbf{TiSe}_2$ exhibits strong electron-phonon coupling, facilitating significant electron locondation. Furthermore, the lattice distortion inherent to this phase promotes the formation of exciton polaritons, enabling their subsequent Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC). Consequently, we anticipate that exciton BEC will induce a superconducting state in this material.

In recent times, online platforms have increasingly adopted text-based systems to facilitate information exchange between system participants, such as authorities and civilians within law enforcement contexts. However, the extent to which these mechanisms effectively achieve their intended purposes remains poorly understood. This study seeks to uncover the hidden functions of these interactive systems by analyzing the actual language used by individuals. Specifically, we investigate the WDLS (Washington State 911 Dispatch Log), a real-world dataset comprising nearly 11 million entries from 911 calls recorded over an eight-year span. By employing a combination of clustering and visualization techniques, we identified eight distinct patterns of language usage. Subsequent analysis of these patterns revealed their characteristics, interrelationships, and temporal behaviors. Furthermore, we examined the names associated with each language cluster to assess whether these groupings align with semantic categories, such as job roles. The findings offer significant implications for enhancing the design and functionality of similar community safety systems.

We examine a two-dimensional superconducting state characterized by nematic symmetry breaking, which supports nodes in the order parameter. Our analysis indicates that spin triplet Cooper pairs forming near a order parameter node can manifest as Pauli paramagnets. This specific paramagnetism stems from the fact that the density of states (DOS) at the Fermi level, arising from the thermal excitation of these paired correlations, fails to exhibit the usual zero-temperature singularity. Consequently, any nymmetric superconductor state that allows triplet pairs adjacent to a node to generate such non-singular DOS will display paramagnetism under these conditions.

End-to-end driving algorithms frequently fail when confronted with adverse weather, poor lighting, or other challenging environmental conditions. This paper introduces a novel framework called Minimax Engaged Learning (MEL), designed to optimize vehicles for the worst-case lighting and weather scenarios while ensuring drivesability. We first define the problem within a Markov decision process and derive a recursive equation for a value function representing minimax performance. Subsequently, we propose the TIM-E agent, which leverages actor-critic methods to solve this definition. Although MEL is designed for broader applications, we demonstrate its specific utility in enhancing autonomous driven during varying light scenarios, for which we supply the necessary dataset. Finally, we outline several adaptations of standard reinforcement learning RL that support our minimax objective.

**Background:** Understanding how information flows through the universe is a central scientific objective. Historically, research in this area has relied on natural signals, such as the human voice, animal vocalizations, and seismic activity generated by earthquakes.

**Objective:** This study examines the development of musical complexity within Western art music spanning from 1750 to 2010.

**Methodology:** The research utilizes an original dataset comprising 1,000 scores, each representing a landmark work from its respective decade. These scores were converted into a unified digital format and assessed for complexity using two distinct metrics: (1) the count of unique trichords (groups of three notes) and ( (2) the application of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) to identify the most probable musical structure.

**Findings:** The analysis reveals a consistent decline in the diversity of trichords over the last 250 years. Additionally, the complexity of the secondary and tertiary musical structures shows a clear downward trend, whereas the primary musical structure remains largely unchanged throughout the period.

**Conclusion:** These results indicate a clear reduction in musical complexity among composers of the 20th and 21st centuries when contrasted with their predecessors from the 18th and 19th centuries.

This study examines the asymptotic properties of a multi-parameter estimation technique based on independent and identically distributed observations drawn from a general distribution. The method utilizes a sequence of bandwidths $h_{n} \rightarrow 0$ and $n P(n) \rightarrow \infty$, where $n$ represents the sample size and $P(n)$ the order of the high-order bias-corrected kernel function. This approach ensures that the method is free from the classical first-order bias constraint, thereby enhancing its accuracy. The research establishes several key results: the asymptotic normality of the estimator, the asymptotic normality of a corresponding bias-corrected high-order version, the asymptotic optimality of the bias-corrected estimator, and the asymptotic optimality of the associated bandwidth selection for both the main and corrected estimators. Furthermore, the methodology is validated through simulated data and a real-world application involving the Israeli Labor Force Survey.

The polars piece at each end of the stick acts as an individual harp tine, and bending the stick alters the inter-tine spacing to adjust for out-of-tune polar items. Reward learning is a fundamental component of Reinforcement Learning (RL) that involves the automated creation of reward functions from historical expert trajectories. However, existing methods are constrained by the need for extensive manual labeling of these trajectories, a process that consumes both money and effort. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces a new Visually Assisted Reward Labeling (VARL) technique that requires human labels only for clustered trajectory sets rather than for every individual path. By integrating this with a clustering algorithm within the RL framework, our approach effectively creates diverse sets for expert and non-expior paths, enabling better discrimination and the generation of more precise reward functions with significantly reduced labeling efforts. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method not only outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions but also saves labeling time by orders of magnitude without compromising, and in fact improving, solution quality.

This study introduces StEIPW, a standardized enhancement to the widely used robust estimator, the inverse probability weighting (IPW) within survey frameworks. The methodology utilizes machine learning algorithms to simultaneously estimate propensity scores and target survey weights, aiming to substantially diminish the variance of the final estimator. We construct the IPWS standardized estimator (StEIPW) using a neural network-based estimator for the survey of household income and wealth in 2019. The $\tau$ lepton is the sole experimentally accessible, yet fully known, non-LEP fourth-generation fermion. Given its pivotal role in establishing the electroweak sector, it serves as an ideal platform for high-precision phenomenological studies. This presentation reviews current experimental status and highlights key open theoretical challenges, particularly those concerning lepton flavor universality violations, anomalous couplings, and properties of the $\tau$-neutrino.

This study presents a comparative analysis of numerical and experimental data regarding flow dynamics in a rotating horizontal annulus. The simulations employ the shallow water equations, while experiments utilize freely falling oils with varying viscosities to model diverse Rossby numbers. The primary objective is the dual validation of experiments against reality and simulations against experimental records, establishing confidence in both datasets for this work. The focus extends to investigating the impact of Rossby number variations on wave generation, specifically examining wave amplitude, radial spacing, and axial angular velocity dependencies. Furthermore, the research analyzes the interplay between angular momentum and potential vorticity to understand the mechanisms of angular velocity shifts across the annulus caused by these waves. The outcomes underscore the critical role of viscosity in determining the system's state, demonstrating that both experimental results and numerical simulations align in this regard.

Standardized analysis of extremes typically relies on a two-stage approach: initially modeling data occurrences via a point process and subsequently analyzing inter-arrival times using either block or peak-over-threshold methods based on conditional distributions. This study introduces a novel, unified reparameterization of the point process that facilitates the simultaneous estimation of both high threshold levels and the conditional distribution. By enabling direct estimation, this method streamlines the workflow and is particularly advantageous for applications requiring real-time monitoring. We validate its efficacy through simulations and a dataset concerning daily rainfall occurrences.

Current fraud detection systems, primarily built on supervised learning, face escalating challenges from evolving and unpredictable fraud tactics. To address this, researchers are exploring unsupervised approaches to identify novel fraud patterns. This study extends those efforts within the framework of reinforcement learning (RL) by investigating decoy environments—also known as offline or surrogate training setups—for fraud detection. We introduce a method to construct deceptive surrogates using an autoencoder to compress state spaces into a lower dimension, followed by an iterative reinforcement algorithm to optimize the policy for evading detection. Additionally, we developed an entropy-based metric to evaluate the effectiveness of these reservoirs in exposing new fraud schemes. The proposed surrogates were tested against real transaction datasets and existing agents to verify performance. Results demonstrate a significant improvement in identifying previously unseen fraud, with detections of 10–20% more cases compared to current state-of-the-art agents.

This paper addresses the one-dimensional thermal equation with dynamic boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the associated operator exhibits logarithmic convexity within the domain of its part, leading to derivations of two distinct observability inequalities for the dual system: one applicable to sensors covering a spatial segment and another for boundary sensors. Furthermore, we establish results regarding the exact and impulse controllability of both the dual and original systems; specifically, we prove exact impulse controllability within the minimal time frame and provide conditions determining its multiplicity. Finally, we prove the existence of impulse and finite-impulse controls for the original system alongside the calculation of the corresponding minimal times and multiplicity orders.

Systematic efforts to detect out-of-domain (OOD) texts are increasingly necessary as models trained on specific domains often struggle with inputs from different sources. This work establishes a unified framework for classification by defining ODD sets through three distinct perspectives: statistical characteristics, semantic features, and syntactic structures. Drawing from current research, the study categorizes ODD texts into three primary categories—(1) the completely unknown domain, (2) the domain partially seen during training, and (3) the intrinsic nature of the domain itself—and analyzes the domain identification task using both qualitative and quantitative methods. The paper concludes with a discussion on the current state of the field, highlighting existing challenges and proposing avenues for future research.

This research introduces a dynamical framework for Brownian molecular ratchet engines whose propulsion relies on inelastic electron tunneling. We establish a unified approach that links the quantum transport of individual electrons to the resulting macroscopic current and power output. Our analysis examines the system's behavior across various temperature regimes and chemical potential ranges, ultimately deriving fundamental constraints on the ultimate dissipation, current, and power achievable by these molecular thermal engines.

Term transducers, which map one instance tree to another instance tree, have long been recognized as a practical extension of tree transducers for handling metaforically nested structures. Recent research by Kallies and Masopust (2020) established that standard tree transducers and term transducers become equivalent in power when restricted to "resynchronization-free" operations, thereby viewing residual synchronization as the specific feature distinguishing the two. However, this work extends that line of inquiry by investigating the "unilateral resynchronization" capability of these devices. Specifically, we define the concept of "one-sided resynchronization" and demonstrate that, unlike standard resynchronization, this one-sided variant allows unilateral resynchronization term transducers to be more potent than non-resynchronized devices on the resynchronization axis.

This paper introduces a generalization of the convolution operation, termed the "generalized convolution." While standard convolutions involve summing products of vector components with indices shifted by a constant offset $k$, the broader form uses an arbitrary function $f(k)$ to determine the weight for each corresponding pair. Although computing this process via brute force requires $O(n^2)$ time, we demonstrate that it can instead be computed in $O(n \log n)$ time employing techniques analogous to those in conventional convolution. These methods rely on applying DFTs to specific vectors $v_k$, where the $i$-th entry corresponds to $f(i)$ evaluated at the $x$ variable. The $i$-th component of the resulting product vector yields the $x$ variable evaluated at the $x$ variable. As an illustration of its utility, we show how to compute the total number of subarrays with sum $0$ in $O(n \log n)$ time, utilizing the proposed algorithm.

The initial identification of the Y-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 marked the discovery of the "smoking gun" for the theoretical evolution of the brown dwarf stellar sequence, establishing the spectral divide between dwarfs and giants at the Y-dwarf/T-dwarf boundary. Since that breakthrough, the object's complex spectral characteristics have been the subject of extensive debate. This study employs the APOLLO code to analyze a new, comprehensive near-infrared spectrum of the dwarf, which integrates data from the Spitzer Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope's NIRCam instrument. Our findings indicate that the data are best fitted by a 1200 K equilibrium temperature model featuring a supersub-solar surface gravity of 2.0 log g, a high metallicity of 0.4 solar units, and the presence of H2SO4 clouds. Although the data allow the co-existence of 1200 K models with 2200 K models under specific conditions, the former offer a more scientifically grounded explanation. This work provides a new set of atmospheric parameters for the "smoking gun," establishing a robust foundation for resolving the dwarf giant distinction within the Y-dwarf class.

To address challenges in identifying likely $0^{-}-$ states, we introduce a comprehensive framework. This approach integrates the QCD sum rule method with a QCD-based Lagrangian describing the characteristics of poles in the scattering amplitude for two pseudoscalar mesons with quantum numbers $J^{PC}=0^{--}$. Our analysis indicates that two distinct poles exist; one aligns with the properties of the $h_b(1^{-}-)$ resonance, whereas the other corresponds to a property consistent with a property consistent with a property consistent with the other corresponds to a property consistent with the $X(8.58)$. The second manifestly falls into the category of a hybrid, exhibiting the characteristics of a meson-meson molecular composite. The second pole, however, displays features inconsistent with a simple molecular interpretation, strongly suggesting it represents a hybrid with quark-antiquark gluon structure.

The recent LHCb determination of the $B_s^{*}\to B_s\gamma$ decay width offers an avenue for testing the Standard Model via radiative $B_s\to B_s\gamma$ decays. This theoretical prediction hinges on the real component of the mass difference, $\Delta M_s$, and the decay amplitude, but is primarily constrained by decays involving charm quarks. Consequently, accurate knowledge of the Breit-Wigner width, $\Gamma_s$, is essential.
