This study addresses the challenge of model-driven reinforcement learning within Markov Decision Processes by focusing on two core objectives: optimality and robustness. To achieve both, we introduce a model-driven policy learning algorithm grounded in learning compact probabilistic transition models. By leveraging these learned models to guide exploration, the algorithm ensures sample efficiency. Furthermore, it guarantees convergence to a policy that maximizes the expected reward, accounting for state and transition uncertainty. We provide a theoretical analysis of the sample complexity and the computational complexity of each iteration, demonstrating that the overall expected return approaches the optimal value in expectation with a number of interactions that is sample efficient. The methodology is validated through experiments on various gridworld scenarios, including a case with an unknown state space dimensionality.

This paper introduces a novel framework for caching and distributed computation that encompasses existing coded caching schemes and is compatible with coded computation, network coding, random linear network, and similar methodologies. The research derives the optimal single-round caching distribution, and for multi-round scenarios, the optimal distribution of cache memory usage. The single-round solution is realized using two mutually exclusive power series distributions, whereas the multi-round memory allocation employs any distribution of series memory size expressed as a sum of at most two non-negative integers. Coded computation and hybrid strategies combining coded caching with other existing methods are all modeled as specific encoded variations. The multi-round encoded caching process is adaptable for universal design using distributed tasks and is applicable to various network topologies, including tree and star networks.

This paper introduces the Scott model of PCF within the univalent type theory framework featuring inductive families and higher inductive types, specifically utilizing the UTTp library in Coq. We establish that the mapping from the free domain into the set of continuous functions is a full embedding, with the converse projection serving as a retraction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that every retro-continuous map admits a representative which is either a strict $\omega$-continuous or a strict $\omega$-strict map. These findings facilitate the embedding of finitely based algebraic lattices, such as the Scott model of PCF, along with the countable initial algebras of the $\omega$-recursion into the set of continuous functions. Additionally, we define a weakly initial algebra for the $\omega$-recursion operator on continuous functions, enabling $\omega$-recursive induction. Our countable order topology aligns with that defined by Hyland and Hyland, thereby establishing an equivalence between their proposed model and ours.
This paper presents a commutative diagram of short exact sequences, which are instrumental in the residue calculation of Eisenstein series for $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$.

Cyber-attacks on mobile robotic arms within smart manufacturing environments could compromise both safety and production output. To mitigate this, we introduce a configuration-aware secure control framework designed to guarantee that the robotic arm remains trapped within a secure safe set, even during potential network intrusions. This approach leverages Control Barrier Functions (CBF) to define the safe set and employs their complement—Complementary Barrier Functions—to construct a configuration-bound "secure control" mechanism. This specific control strategy ensures that any trajectory originating inside the safe set never breaches its boundaries. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this control strategy is merely a unique, time-varying, and strictly monototone transformation of the nominal control input, a property that maintains the arm's safe set as a strict invariant. Under the assumption of a configuration-aware secure control scheme, we establish that the nominal control input undergoes a monototone transformation to guarantee safety. Finally, we validate our findings through simulations on a mobile robotic arm.

Natural language processing (NLP) has seen a rise in interest due to the abundance of unstructured text and the urgent need to create concise, accurate text summaries. This research presents an extractive approach to summarization that utilizes graphs to identify and rank key sentences. The methodology involves constructing a graph where each node corresponds to a sentence, and edges represent the logical connections between them; the resulting sentence rankings are derived by calculating the strength of these links using a dedicated linking architecture. This approach was evaluated using the "Dailymail" dataset, achieving an ROUGE-L score of 0.6081, which places it in the top tier compared to other algorithms.

We examine a geometry where two nonlinear couplers interact with a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC), utilizing mean-field theory to analyze its properties. Interaction between the couplers and the system enables a nonlinear coupling mechanism between them for the injected atoms. We demonstrate that, contrary to standard linear cases, the couplers can be simultaneously resonant with both non-resonant transitions—specifically, a resonant transition for one system component and a non-resonant, yet nonlinearly mediated, transition for the other—even when these physical transitions differ significantly in energy. Through analysis of two distinct configurations, the role of nonlinear quantum interference in controlling the spectral response is highlighted.

"Wen and Xu recently demonstrated that five distinct non-degenerate meromorphic maps from a complete K\"{a}hler manifold $M$ into the projective space $\mathbb{P}^N$ ($N\geq 6$)$,$ where no four maps share the same target variety, must be mutually distinct in the sense of value sharing, thereby generalizing a finding by Chen and Zaleski. Building on this result, we further prove the following: let $F_1, \dots, F_q$ be such distinct non-degenerate meromorphic maps sharing a common small family $\mathcal{F}$; if $q$ satisfies $q\left(N-q+1\right)\left(N+q+2\right)/4\geq N+2$, then the maps are value-disjoint except possibly for images contained within the set of maps in the set $F\in\mathcal{S}$."

Determining the number and nature of solutions to polynomial systems is a fundamental challenge with broad applications across engineering and scientific domains. Existing methods for counting polynomials' nontrivial locuses generally fall into two categories: approaches rooted in real algebraic geometry that rely on tools like Sturm chains, and algorithmic methods based on complex algebraic geometry often employing techniques such as the nontrivial bound. This paper introduces an algorithm that leverages the signature to compute nontrivial locuses, capable of handling systems comprising multiple and varied dimensional polynomial sets. This approach is adaptable to diverse configurations of polynomial systems and, upon completion, yields comprehensive signature-based views of solution spaces.

This paper addresses Tur\'an\'s Tetrahedron Problem, first introduced in 1941, which seeks a subset of points within the unit cube $[0,1]^d$ maximizing the product of pairwise Euclidean distances. While prior estimates for the largest such product in the unit cube were established by Balasubramanian, Saha, and Sudbery for $d=3$ and generally for even dimensions, this study presents improved upper and lower bounds for the case of $d=4$. Specifically, the authors propose a configuration of over one million points on the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^4$ that establishes a tighter bound of approximately $0.04183$ (precisely $\frac{1}{\sqrt{24}}$) for the maximum product. Furthermore, the work introduces a computational framework that can verify whether an arbitrary arrangement of unit-sphere points in $\mathbb{R}^4$ constitutes a Tetrahedron-free set, a capability leveraged to execute a rigorous search across the unit sphere. This exhaustive search yields a refined upper bound of $0.04180$ on the problem.

When rendering thin objects like lines and text at low resolutions, edges often appear jagged due to spatial aliasing. While traditional anti-aliasing techniques mitigate this visually, they can cause other issues, including blurred output, the obscuring of geometric junctions, and inconsistencies in line width. To address these specific problems, this paper proposes a novel, effective spatial anti-aliasing approach tailored for vector maps. The method introduces a line-aware rendering framework that distinguishes between primary line segments and their intersections. It calculates intersection points precisely based on the geometric connections between these lines and uses them as masks to preserve visual sharpness at join points. Furthermore, by assigning unique, calculated dither patterns to both the lines and the masks, this technique achieves visually uniform results.

We have analyzed the topological and spectral characteristics of 111 pulsar emission shells within the Milky Way, utilizing data from the Fermi-LAT collaboration. This study provides the most comprehensive census to date of pulsar shell remnants across the 50 MeV to 300 GeV spectrum. Our findings indicate that the spectral properties of these emission shells are diverse, with the majority (80%) exhibiting a break or cutoff in their energy distribution. Furthermore, we observe a significant correlation between the spectral cutoff and the age of the associated nebula for objects younger than approximately $10^5$ years, suggesting that the terminal shocks formed by young pulsars dictate this limit. Additionally, the spatial distribution of pulsar shells is highly non-uniform; they cluster along the Galactic plane with a pronounced latitude offset of approximately 1.5°. This trend aligns with the known age-dependent migration of pulsars away from the plane, supporting the observation that older shells are found at greater galactic latitudes.

The categorization of weather conditions is essential for numerous applications, ranging from agriculture and construction to navigation and logistics. While various techniques exist to classify weather using videos or images, they are constrained by limited generalization capabilities. This study introduces a novel dataset comprising 1,500 images meticulously hand-labeled across ten distinct weather categories. To facilitate comparative analysis, we conducted extensive experiments evaluating multiple Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures, beginning with established models and progressing through enhanced configurations. Furthermore, to mitigate common issues such as vanishing gradients and feature extraction difficulties often encountered in deep learning, we implemented specific solutions including residual connections, batch normalization, and a new weight update mechanism inspired by human cognitive learning. Testing on our dataset demonstrated that the improved models significantly boosted classification accuracy, rising from 68.4% with the original structures to 80.2%.

This study examines how scientific and economic understandings of climate change intersect with societal norms surrounding the topic. It utilizes survey data from German citizens to analyze the relationship between perceptions of scientific and economic consensus (or lack thereof) and adherence to societal standards regarding climate change. The research highlights a distinct difference: trust in scientific consensus shows a stronger link to conformity with social standards, whereas beliefs about economic consensus exhibit this association only among individuals with average or below-average educational attainment.

Soft grippers offer significant advantages over rigid counterparts, including superior force distribution, high dexterity, and durability, yet their control remains difficult due to inherent nonlinearities, infinite-dimensional dynamics, and sensitivity to disturbances. This study introduces a virtual modeling and regulation strategy for multi-fingered soft grippers utilizing Koopman operator theory. The method begins by defining a nonlinear finite-element model of the soft structure, mapping it via coordinate transformation into the domain of the linearized Koopman operator. Next, a discrete-time, discrete-time-like or hybrid-type linearized representation of the gripper is derived using reduced-order techniques based on proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and snapshot decomposition. The resulting infinite-dimensional Koopman operator is then approximated as a finite matrix. Finally, an iterative learning control (ILC) scheme is implemented on this linearized, reduced-order model to optimize contact force distribution and loading patterns for a given input trajectory. Validation through both finite-element simulations and physical experiments confirms the approach's efficacy, demonstrating that the ILC strategy significantly enhances performance by leveraging the successful linearization and order-reduction of the underlying dynamical system.

Building on the findings of "On the Dynamics of Gradient Descent over Spherical Layers" by Saxe et al. (2018), this work extends and unifies the analysis of gradient descent dynamics in single-hidden layer neural models. It establishes an invariant for these dynamics applicable to broader loss functions, including those that are non-convex. By administering specific lower and upper bounds on the gradient's projection, this study derives constraints for the evolution of first- and second-layer weights alongside hidden unit norms. The findings generalize a previously identified boundary for the solution existence limit and are sufficient to guarantee Riemann-manifold gradient descent convergence for specific composite loss functions.

We report the discovery of a new, distant radio source, J2102+6015, with a redshift of z=4.575, identified through follow-up observations of the Lyman-break galaxy candidate GN-z11. This radio galaxy exhibits a luminosity of L1.4GHz = 1.1 x 10^30 W, making it the second-brightest known source at this redshift, with a linear size of approximately 14 kpc. Its spectrum shows a flat slope (alpha = -0.1 +/- 0.3), indicative of a young population of magnetic sources free from significant spectral aging. Additionally, its radio morphology is simple, lacking the complex double-lobed structure typical of lower-redshift galaxies, which supports the conclusion that its radio jets are in the initial phase of development.

Non-Small-Cell Lung Carcinoma (NSCLC) stands as the prevalent form of lung malignancy, characterized by a poor prognosis due to a lack of effective treatment options. Recent research indicates that imaging features can assist in predicting outcomes, though this capability is not universal across all patient demographics. We propose a deep learning framework that integrates radiological data from CT scans and pathological data from Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) stained slides to forecast Overall Survival (OS) times. This multimodal approach enhances OS estimation accuracy by capturing comprehensive information from distinct data sources. We evaluated the model using a dataset from the Kaggle NSCC Challenge, which included 1,000 annotated slides and corresponding 3D lung CT scans. Evaluation metrics demonstrated that a simple radiological model achieved an AUC of 0.63, whereas our proposed integration improved this to an AUC of 0.68.

In recent years, incorporating natural language into Reinforcement Learning (RL) has gained significant traction. This study presents a systematic review of Authenticated Language-based Sequential Decision Making (ALSD), a domain recently renamed from Natural Language-assisted Sequential Decision Making (NLDS). We outline the background necessary for understanding ALSD, review various techniques employed to encode natural language within RL frameworks, and assess the pros and cons alongside the performance outcomes of these approaches. Additionally, we identify current challenges and opportunities within ALSD to guide future research efforts. Finally, this paper proposes a pending classification system for ALSD literature to aid in the categorization of related academic work.

Machine learning models are increasingly valuable for analyzing large datasets and solving complex problems in astronomy. This study focuses on reconstructing the cosmological matter power spectrum from quasars using neural networks. The data employed consists of 1000 mock quasar lightcones derived from N-body simulations combined with a fitting of the halo occupation distribution to model quasars. These simulations were used to train a U-Net network, which successfully achieved an $r^2$ score of 0.98 in predicting power spectra. The matter power spectrum was found to be most sensitive to quasars residing in galaxy clusters, whereas isolated quasars contributed only marginally. The same ML architecture demonstrated success in recovering the density energy spectrum from individual quasars' quasi-power spectra. However, the resulting recovery of the matter power spectrum from these density energy signals exhibited an $r^2$ score of approximately 0.65, indicating that quasars do not fully capture the matter distribution. The study concludes that the current model achieves optimal performance and that incorporating additional small-scale physical processes, such as those involving dark matter halo substructures, would likely degrade the model's accuracy.

Let $h$ denote an arbitrary finite-dimensional vector space, and let $W(h)$ represent the algebra comprising linear operators on $h$'s algebra of polynomial functions that differentiate this space differentially. This paper investigates the module theory specific to $W(h)$, focusing on the algebraic structure of derivative differential operators acting on $h$. 

This study extends previous work from Zeeman and others who examined similar properties for $Sp(2n)$, applying it here to the broader context of $U(h)$, the universal enveloping algebra associated with linear operators on $h$. 

Assuming a module status for $M$ over algebra $U(h)$, we demonstrate that if the module is vacant (trivial), then a specific graded structure emerges within the module space itself. This structure is established via an isomorphism between the module $M$ and a tensor product formed by $U(h)$ and another module $N$, where the latter appears as the module quotient. 

Furthermore, we explore the concept of vertex algebras constructed specifically from polynomial functions on $h$, analyzing their vertex operator algebraic structures in relation to the Lie algebras of differential operators.

Twitter Sentiment Analysis (TSW) involves assessing the sentiment of Twitter messages. Over recent years, this research has gained significant traction, primarily due to two factors: the widespread adoption of micro-blogging platforms like social networking sites, and the availability of open-source sentiment datasets. While platforms such as Twitter offer vast volumes of user-generated data, only a small fraction can be definitively classified as positive, negative, or neutral. Consequently, this study introduces an Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework designed to automatically annotate sentiments for an unlabeled dataset comprising 31 million tweets. By leveraging this pre-trained model, the research achieves superior accuracy compared to other state-of-the-art approaches when benchmarked against standard datasets.

We introduce LLaDialog, an open-domain, dialogue-focused language model developed through the fine-tuning of GPT-3 on the newly developed CoChat training set. This dataset comprises over 1.5 million high-quality sample dialogues, generated by the HuggingFace dataset curation team through interactions between GPT-3 and human annotators. We have made LLaDialog fully accessible to the public via the HuggingFace Databricks. Despite its compact size relative to other open-dialogue resources, extensive evaluation results confirm that our dataset successfully generates coherent, contextually relevant, and engaging conversational turns. Consequently, the model produced by fine-tuning achieves performance that significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art dialogues in terms of engagement and understanding, while also meeting or exceeding the standards of human-level interaction.

A novel form of gravitational wave memory emerges when linearized perturbations around Minkowski spacetime interact with an arbitrary matter distribution, representing the permanent, non-radiative deformation caused by radiation. We investigate whether this memory effect, when generalized beyond specific scenarios, could constitute a random GW backdrop detectable by observatories like LIGO and Virgo. Our findings indicate that while this phenomenon might be stochastic, its amplitude falls significantly short of current detection thresholds established by these instruments.

We introduce a novel mechanism where SUSY-breaking occurs via a first-order phase transition involving a complex scalar field. The vacuum expectation value (VEV) of this field decays at the high energy scale of $10^{15}$ GeV during the process, providing sufficient scale for leptogenesis. This same scale can also generate a significant peak in gravitational waves due to the transition's violence, making it detectable by future detectors like DECIGO and BBO. Additionally, we demonstrate that supersymmetric black holes could form directly from the energy density of the transition itself.

Emergent communication aims to transmit the minimal necessary information for reliable decision-making at the receiver, an objective that becomes increasingly vital in bandwidth-constrained 6G environments. This study introduces a novel framework termed SemComC, which integrates neuro-symbolic causal inference with signaling games to achieve efficient semantic signaling. The proposed method employs logical rules to decompose input data into fundamental features and their causal relationships, while an neuro-symbolic architecture jointly optimizes both encoding and decoding processes. Furthermore, the incorporation of causal structures allows the semcomc model to reduce reliance on high-fidelity transmission in data-rich areas while dynamically adjusting to preserve fidelity in data-sparse regions through learned causal reasoning. Real-world validation using natural images and medical CT scans demonstrates that semcomc surpasses existing state-of-the-art semantic communication schemes.

Predicting new terms between pairs of similar concepts is a vital task for applications like semantic web and information retrieval. This study introduces a dual-phase approach. In the initial phase, the problem is modeled as a classification task where the objective is to distinguish between terms that enhance (positive) versus those that do not fit (negative) into a concept bank, utilizing an established hybrid class. This classification step employs the Naive Bayes algorithm to leverage labeled datasets. Subsequently, in the second phase, the problem shifts to finding terms with specific characteristics within the positive dataset by applying dimensionality reduction to reduce feature complexity, followed by ranking using cosine similarity based on reduced vectors to identify the most relevant candidates. The classification stage was executed with the Weka machine learning tool, while dimensionality reduction and final selection were conducted via the Scikit-learn Python library. Testing on the existing TWIST dataset confirmed the method's efficacy, achieving an 80.4% accuracy rate in prediction.

Session-based recommendation aims to predict a subsequent item within a user's browsing session using only current session information, a task that has recently gained prominence due to its efficiency in private scenarios. This study introduces a new model called TP-SR, which enhances recommendations within sessions by merging two distinct mechanisms: (1) merging sessions based on query similarity and (2) employing rank representations for item sequences. By integrating these components, TP-SR addresses two specific limitations found in prior research. First, it utilizes query-based session merging to offer a broader view of user interests early in a session, thereby enriching recommendation quality with more historical context. Second, it leverages a novel representation using item ranks to capture both the item's relevance and its positional significance in the sequence. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that the TP-SR model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art session-based recommendation methods.

Active particles that possess shape anisotropy are a defining feature of numerous living colloids. While their internal energy supply drives persistent motion, their irregular geometry dictates a specific orientation, making orientation-dependent (or dipolar) activation a prevalent mechanism. In this study, we formulate a continuum framework to investigate the dynamics of such oriented active colloids by examining their response to activity gradients. Our analysis demonstrates that under these conditions, a steady-state superdiffusion emerges, characterized by a long-tail probability density function (PDF) and a mean-squared-displacement (MSD) scaling linearly with time. Furthermore, we examine how the interplay between dipolar activation and probabilitic environments influences dynamical traits, with experimental data supporting these theoretical predictions.

The approach employs a new type of non-structured, multi-dimensional, and conforming mesh that effectively captures the geometry of any number of fractures, regardless of their orientation, complexity, or orientation. This method utilizes a two-level strategy: the fractures are discretized using a mesh with high local mesh size $H$, while the surrounding matrix is simulated with a global, coarser matrix having local mesh size $h$ ($h \ll h$). This hierarchical discretization significantly lowers computational costs. This study introduces two innovative methods designed to maintain cellular formations within autonomous drone swarms while avoiding collisions. The first approach utilizes registration techniques centered on alignment of the major and minor axes, along with the rotation and elongation derived from a covariance matrix. Our analysis demonstrates that this method effectively preserves the cell's core architecture and guides the robots along the shortest possible routes to reach their target positions. The second approach employs general point-set registration, capable of handling cells composed of both convex and concave configurations. Findings indicate this strategy successfully directs robots into their designated formation points and maintains the cellular structure's integrity. Furthermore, both strategies ensure that all cells within the overall layout remain mutually non-overlapping.

This study addresses a mean-field optimization problem involving dynamic equations with delay and driven by fractional Brownian motion within the framework of lower semicontinuous convex functionals. Specifically, we first establish the existence of optimal solutions by leveraging the uniform convexity properties of these functionals and the properties of normalized measures on the space of normalized probability measures on a Polish space. Subsequently, by introducing a novel weak derivative for the composition of finite-dimensional functions with stochastic delay equations with driven by fractional Brownian motion, we derive the Frechet derivative of the composition of finite-dimensional functions and these processes. Finally, the paper provides necessary and sufficient conditions for optimality by defining a specific weak derivative of these functions and the corresponding probability measures on the space of normalized probability measures on a Polish space.

This study investigates a non-self-adjoint Dirac operator featuring a periodic potential. By investigating its associated eigenvalue problem, we observe that its band structure mirrors that of a Hill's operator. We establish the existence of an infinite subset of periodic potentials capable of transforming the system into a finite-band operator, akin to a lattice model. For these specific cases, we derive the explicit eigenvalues and their multiplicities. Additionally, we illustrate the existence of stochastic systems within a parameter space that form an open set. Finally, we present explicit计算公式 for the energy of these finite-band periodic solutions.

This paper introduces a novel two-tier heterogeneous Vehicular Network (VANet) model, which integrates Roadside Units (RSUs) and vehicle-based relays. The primary objective is to determine the optimal placement for these components to maximize overall network capacity. To address this, we first construct a stochastic geometry framework based on a Poisson Point Process (PPP) representing the spatial distribution of vehicles. Within this model, cars acting as data forwarders are categorized into two distinct types: those equipped with a single wireless interface and those acting as multi-hop relays for vehicles lacking direct connectivity. Second, we develop a Car-following framework to analyze the density of vehicle populations in both single- and multi-hop scenarios. Subsequently, we derive the probability density function (PDF) of the aggregate network capacity by examining the spatial clustering of vehicles, the link-level signal-to-interference ratio (SIR), and the resulting Shannon capacity formula. Finally, we evaluate the proposed analytical results against Monte-Carlo simulations, demonstrating that the derived theoretical derivations align closely with simulated data.

Although Wikipedia functions as a primary source for many knowledge bases, it frequently contains entries that are factually incorrect, poorly written, or overly brief. Such low-quality articles undermine the reliability of generated responses based on its content, even when those answers appear valid. Current moderation relies on community volunteers and automated tools, yet many problematic items evade detection due to the sheer volume of updates and the limited capacity of volunteers. This paper proposes a novel system that leverages established patterns in editing behaviors to classify the "low quality" status of revisions, facilitating more efficient tagging. Testing on a West-European Wikipedia instance with 99.6% English usage demonstrated that the system achieves 84.1% precision and 84.4% recall. Future applications could benefit from deploying this system across diverse, large-scale Wikipedias and integrating it with automated monitoring pipelines to improve user experience.

Transfer learning offers a pathway to superior model performance by utilizing external knowledge, yet establishing transferability remains difficult when examining zero-shot scenarios with black-box decision-making processes. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a method for transferring knowledge to a decision-focused black-box system through an evolutionary process. It enhances how external knowledge is transferred zero-shot by employing a specialized fitness function that balances two criteria: the black-box utility of knowledge and how similarly the knowledge source aligns with the target domain. This approach was tested using neural networks as both the black-box framework and a set of external models. Results demonstrate that this technique outperforms pure random transfer and, most significantly, outperforms models fine-tuned specifically for comparison benchmarks.

The LHCb collaboration reports the first observation of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decays, yielding a significance of 9.2$\sigma$. Evidence (greater than 3$\sigma$) for the related process $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^*{}^0 K^0_L$ is also presented. Measurements of the related parameters $\bar{D}^0\to J/\psi\pi^+\pi^-\pi^-\pi^+\}$ and $\bar{D}^0\to J/\psi\pi^+\pi^+\}$ are used to measure the branching fractions $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L) = (4.4\pm 0.7\pm 0.7)\times 10^{-3}$ and $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^*{}^0 K^0_L) = (1.7\pm 0.6\pm 0.4)\times 10^{-3}$.

This paper explores T-duality geometrically within the framework of twisted tori—encompassing both torus bundles with torus connections and non-unimodular tori—specifically through the lens of twisted torus T-duality. By employing the Hilbert class space associated with a twisted tori along with its associated dual space as building blocks, we construct all possible T-duality transformations applicable to a given torus. For a specific case involving a simply connected, 4-dimensional, 2-dimensionally twisted tori, these constructions utilize fourth-level class spaces of second type together with spatial geometric descriptions of the first kind; specifically, by defining the topological invariants as the Euler characteristic and the first integral, one can uniquely specify the topological structure. The authors further demonstrate the application of their method to the Hall class space space within theoretical physics models.

Current multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) approaches often struggle to generalize to unsolved tasks because they lack the specific experience required to tackle them. While distillation-based methods address this by other agents to solve issues, these solutions fail to capture the task's essence when the tasked agents do not already know how to resolve them. In this paper, we propose Co-Observation Learning (COL) for distributed multi-agent systems. COL enables a group of agents to collectively acquire a task even in the absence of individual expertise through cooperative information sharing. By leveraging simultaneous observations, COL fosters effective collaboration and accelerates learning. We demonstrate COL's efficacy on complex navigation challenges within both simple and complex network topologies.

This paper addresses a novel methodology for calculating the distance of uniquely decodable, prefix, and suffix-free codes. We introduce an efficient algorithm that determines $d(C)$ for a given code set $C$ in $O((d(C)+1)|C| \log |C|)$ time using $O((d(C)+1)|C|)$ space. Compared to the previously fastest approach—which operated in $O((d(C)+1)|C| \log |C|)$ time with $O((d(C)+1)|C|)$ spatial complexity—this new method represents a linear improvement in both time and space relative to the distance factor. We also introduce two additional algorithms with complexities of $O(|C| \log |C|)$ time and $O(d(C)|C|)$ space, as well as one with $O(|C| \log |C|)$ time and $O(d(C)|C|)$ space. The proposed methods are demonstrated through a practical implementation targeting the measurement of distance in Polyalphabetic Aribtrary Concatenation (PAC) codes.

We introduce a novel system designed to track the hand and head, along with their associated movements, while interacting with objects in the natural environment, utilizing only raw point cloud sequences captured by an uncalibrated consumer-grade monocular RGB camera. This system reconstructs both the user's hand geometry and deformations through cycle-based constraint optimization, while simultaneously performing semantic segmentation and dynamic mesh reconstruction of the target object to explicitly model surface boundaries. A key innovation is the ability to jointly model the hand and object deformations, a capability that enables more precise tracking than prior methods. We have applied this system to record and analyze data from two distinct experiments: one mapping the human hand and its deformations while grasping a banana, and another recording a research assistant's hand, its deformations, and head motions while handling a mechanical arm within a laboratory setting.

The work focuses on classifying finite non-Zassenhaus Coxeter groups defined by tail triangles with angles proportional to $(2, 2, 1)$, specifically those possessing crystallographic graphs of grades 4 and interlacing values of 2.

This paper introduces a deep learning method to estimate the robot end-effector's position within the depth camera field, accounting for the camera's orientation relative to the object. Accurate pose estimation is essential for tasks like remote manipulation; however, traditional methods relying on calibration are often hindered by difficulties in precisely positioning robots and depth sensors, as well as variability in tasks due to lack of a fixed base. To overcome these constraints, we developed an approach that learns optimal camera-robot alignment and depth-based pose estimation simultaneously. By training our model on unmarked data collected from the camera at various robot joints configurations, we demonstrate that the system effectively generalizes to new cameras and robots without requiring explicit labels.

This work investigates how to identify causal treatment effects in the presence of interference within our proposed k-nearest interference (KNNI) framework. In this model, a unit's response is determined by its own received treatment alongside the treatments of its k nearest neighbor interference units. We propose two new algorithms for detecting whether a specific k-nearest interference assumption holds. The first method analyzes treatment responses by aggregating the treatment assignments of the k nearest neighbors using logistic regression. The second method leverages graph convolutional networks to identify suitable values of k and response functions that effectively summarize treatment from the interference group. Extensive experiments on both simulated data and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that our methods are effective at validating the KNNI assumptions and uncovering true causal treatment effects.

We calculate neutrino emission rates resulting from dark matter (fermionic or bosonic) annihilation into neutrinos inside neutron stars, where dark matter pairs scatter off nucleons mediated by pseudoscalar operators. By employing the worldline formalism for both the computation of photon and vertex functions and the evaluation of the four-neutrino operator, we achieve a more transparent and simplified analytical structure. This approach facilitates the rigorous incorporation of finite temperature and finite density conditions, a step critical for accurate modeling in dense stellar environments. Our findings indicate that dark matter emission rates generally surpass standard thermal neutrino emissivity, except in the specific scenario involving neutron self-annihilation mediated by pseudoscalars, where they remain comparable. Consequently, dark matter contributions could dominate the total luminosity of cooling neutron stars.

The primary objective of the Space Telescopes and Satellite Systems (STST) initiative is the development of innovative space telescopes and the analysis of their resulting data. A key scientific focus within this program is the application of high-resolution imaging to large-scale structures in the cosmos, with cosmic shear emerging as a leading technique for studying the expansion history of the universe. This paper introduces ShapePipe, a novel, flexible, and scalable workflow designed specifically for measuring galaxy shapes. ShapePipe leverages the scientific potential of large-scale imaging by streamlining shape measurements. It is a versatile pipeline written in Python, utilizing the AstroImageProcess framework and the ASPIRE algorithm. AstroImageProcess provides the necessary abstraction to handle diverse image formats, while ASPIRE (AStronomy PIpe End-to-end Resampling) is a specialized algorithm for PSF deconvolution. The shape measurement workflow within this framework is fully modular, allowing users to swap in different components, such as alternative algorithms, at will. We demonstrate the pipeline's efficacy and flexibility through a case study of UNIONS/CFIS data, a high-resolution survey covering 1,000 square degrees conducted by the NASA Synchronous Imaging Surveyor. The study shows ShapePipe successfully deconvolves images using the ASPIRE algorithm and performs shape recovery, resulting in a significant improvement in shear estimation accuracy.

The field-induced alignment of spin systems toward classical, ordered states offers a practical approach to studying quantum phase transitions. Recently, a breakthrough occurred when researchers at Vienna's University demonstrated that adjusting magnetic fields in the Heisenberg magnet barium copper phosphate ($BaCuO_2$) could simulate the effect of varying quantum coupling constants. This allows for the direct observation of the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition—a phenomenon predicted theoretically but previously unverified experimentally. By measuring spin correlations across multiple planes within the material, the study confirmed a three-dimensional restoration of long-range order when the effective coupling constant decreases due to aligned external fields. The findings, published in *Nature Physics*, provide the first experimental validation of the BKT transition in a solid-state system, confirming a rare case where distinct quantum systems can exhibit identical physical behaviors.

This study examines the evolution of a non-equilibrium thermal system by integrating Tsallis' non-equilibrium statistical mechanics with the holographic dark matter model. We specifically analyze the energy density of Tsallis holographic dark vitality (THQD), noting that it can exist in either real or complex representations. Focusing on the complex form, we demonstrate that it naturally decomposes into two components: the first represents the kinetic energy derived from the expansion of the universe, while the second captures the potential energy, which we interpret as the source of dark matter. We further analyze the properties of this model using the Complex Form of the Quintessence (CFQ) framework. In CFQ, the dark energy equation-of-state parameter oscillates between -1 and positive infinity, allowing the kinetic and potential energy components to be non-zero, unlike in standard quintessence models. This analysis allows us to derive the real and imaginary parts of THQD and their respective components explicitly in terms of the CFQ parameters. Finally, we assess the physical viability of our theoretical construction through analyses involving thermodynamics, stability, and the scaling behavior of these energy components.

Pseudo-random number generators (PRNGs) are essential for a wide range of security applications, yet they remain vulnerable to exploitation because their outputs can be predicted or their states reversed. Although researchers have explored various physical sources for more authentic randomness, including PRNGs that harvest entropy from SRAM bit transitions during power-up, these solutions still face risks of side-channel exposure and incomplete unpredictability. To address this, we introduce TuRaN, a novel true Random Number Service that generates genuine randomness by running SRAMs at significantly reduced supply voltages. This approach creates a environment so chaotic that memory access results become entirely stochastic. We have validated this strategy through both SPICE simulations and actual experiments, demonstrating that SRAM operations under severe voltage constraints produce data characterized by high entropy and independence. TuRaN successfully deployed on three distinct commercial off-the-shelf processors, achieving speeds comparable to leading software-based methods while offering vastly superior security guarantees.

This study introduces a new class of nonvolatile resistive memory devices, termed molecular self-assembled monolayer (SAM) resistive switch (RS) neurons, which utilize self-organized layers of organic molecules on silicon. These devices are formed through the self-electrochemical deposition of a nanometer-thick, conductive, and tunable atomic metal island onto the RS surface, effectively acting as a single-electron transistor (SET) island. This setup places a single molecular layer between the electron source, drain, and an electrostatic gate situated beneath the silicon. By integrating the SET transistor with a dipole-based single-electron tunneling switch (SMRS), the device functions as a resistive switch neuron capable of switching based on individual electrons. We present the design, modeling, and characterization of these components, alongside an analysis of their combined physics. Ultimately, we evaluate the performance of these hybrid RS neurons, discussing their specific advantages and viable applications in future memory systems.

Feynman diagrammatic techniques are employed to investigate transient phenomena in quantum field theory. While these tools offer valuable qualitative insights, their quantitative application is often hindered by complex mathematical calculations. This study introduces a novel application of the causal depiction approach to trace the evolution of field theory systems depicted in standard Feynman diagrams. We demonstrate how this method streamlines the computation of multi-loop figures, particularly by simplifying the implementation of momentum conservation laws. Additionally, we outline a procedure for evaluating these diagrams using standard numerical integration methods. As a proof of concept, applying this technique to modified, computationally tractable Feynman diagrams yields results that align closely with traditional QFT calculations performed via standard software.

We investigate composite stars that emerge from the interaction between a bosonic sector (sigma, omega, and rho mesons) and fermionic quarks, constrained by the MIT and MIT charge conjugate (NJL) bag equations. These inhomogeneous matter configurations arise due to repulsive interactions among mesons and are formed as bound states resulting from glue between composite fermions and anti-fermions. Specifically, we examine two distinct classes of these objects: magnetically charged stars composed of composite nucleons, which result from a network of nucleon-nucleus forces, and neutral stars made of composite nucleons formed via nucleon-nucleus binding. To determine their properties, we analyze the interplay between long-range mesonic fields and short-range nucleonic forces, employing a variational method to construct the ground-state wave function for nucleons within a self-consistent framework.

Notably, our findings reveal enhanced transparency and control over light speed when the system operates in a negative motion sideband regime compared to the standard sideband approach.

Recent studies have demonstrated that ultrathin crystalline oxides grown on mismatched substrates can exhibit x-ray absorption fine structure (XFS) signatures indicating both in-plane rotation and out-of-plane tilting of crystal axes. While the in-plane rotation is readily understood as a direct consequence of lattice mismatch, the mechanism behind the out-of-plane component remained obscure. This article clarifies that such dual signatures arise from the inherent properties of epitaxial strain within these epimismatch systems, provided the oxide film is thick enough. Specifically, the film's interface with the substrate enforces the substrate's out-of-plane lattice parameters at the boundary, while the outer surface experiences rotation around this axis in the plane. Because epitaxial films often show significant anisotropic thermal expansion coefficients, the interaction between this rotation and the fixed boundary condition generates a measurable tilt. Consequently, the magnitude of this out-of-plane component scales with the oxide layer's thickness and the magnitude of in-plane rotational angle, alongside the intrinsic anisotropic thermal expansion. The presented analysis offers a comprehensive framework for interpreting such effects in epitaxial oxide layers and similar substrate-mismatch scenarios, extending naturally to other spectroscopic methods.

Laser cooling within all-optical arrays presents a highly controllable platform for investigating the dynamics of dissipative quantum systems. This study introduces a novel theoretical framework that merges a first-principls master equation approach with a mapping technique to the driven quantum harmonic lattice. Applying this method to optical lattice beams, we reveal a distinct transition in system dynamics: shifting from a standard thermalization phase to a regime where atoms either clump together or disperse. Furthermore, by integrating these findings with a Stochastic Trajectory method, we demonstrate the ability to precisely regulate the mean position and variance of an atom through adjustments to laser parameters.

This study examines how cryptocurrency dependencies evolve over time, moving beyond standard linear correlations to incorporate less typical higher-order connections. Utilizing pairwise and nonpairwise entropy measures, the authors analyze cryptocurrency market dynamics across two datasets: one containing higher-frequency crypto trading data from 2013 to 2020, and another comprising daily returns for major cryptocurrencies from 2018 to 2022. Key findings indicate a stronger strength and more persistent nature of these dependencies during market downturns. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that while volatility significantly impacts linear and pairwise correlations, its effect on higher-order dependencies is minimal. Finally, the authors observe that the dependencies among prominent cryptocurrencies remain stable regardless of the time frequency analyzed.

Molecular clusters consisting of sulfuric acid and water are essential for atmospheric acid deposition and particle nucleation. While previous studies have extensively analyzed their structural and thermodynamic properties using various computational approaches, these efforts typically neglect the significance of zero-point motion (ZPM). This study addresses that gap by incorporating ZPM analysis into Møller-Plesset perturbation theory calculations for small H₂SO₄·(H₂O)ₙ₆ (n = 1–6) cluster systems. We evaluated its impact on structural geometry, reaction energetics associated with proton transfer, and the resulting proton affinity trends. Findings indicate that ZPM causes minor structural adjustments but substantially alters the energetics of proton transfer reactions. Consequently, ZPM softens the distinction between the basic sulfuric acid·(H₂O)ₙ and protonated basic water (i.e., (H₂SO₄)ₙ₊₁) forms. These effects also weaken the proton affinity trends as a function of water cluster size.

Additionally, specific techniques are examined to determine, under specific conditions of relative recognizability, whether two such compactifications can be considered relatively known. This method finds application in various fields, specifically within the study of groups with a length function and in the analysis of geometrically finite groups with a convex core.

The presence of a Hall response in systems exhibiting zero net charge transport signifies deviations from Einstein relations and Einstein- like behaviors, moving beyond traditional hydrodynamic frameworks. Within a phenomenological study, it is shown that the magnitude of this response offers a measure of how severely such general hydrodynamic theories fail. Moreover, the amplitude of the response imposes rigorous constraints on the admissible kinetic mechanisms for neutral particles. Therefore, the thermal Hall response serves as a vital tool for distinguishing between competing theories of effective motion and particle interaction, a utility illustrated here through applications to hydrophobic interactions where particles experience effects similar to gravitational analogues.

A central challenge in deep learning theory is understanding why simple models often suffice, even when training data is noisy. We introduce a method to analyze the complexity of both neural network and piecewise polynomial classifiers using average description length (ADL), a metric from the description length framework. Leveraging this tool, we examine a standard result from prior research: that the neural network's generalization error is bounded by its training error plus a term proportional to the network's capacity. Our investigation reveals that similar capacity-based ADL bounds can be derived for classifiers with a fixed number of pieces, providing an alternative approach. Finally, we explore how the notion of capacity influences the generalization error of these simpler classifiers.

Most existing copula-based modeling approaches for bivariate datasets focus exclusively on capturing marginal univariate distributions through density estimation. In our work, we introduce a novel class of marginal dependence models that can be utilized alongside standard copulas to fit full distributions for bivariate data. Specifically, these models enable the estimation of parameters within copulas to proceed independently of this new framework. Our approach offers a computationally efficient framework that is particularly advantageous when dealing with massive datasets. We validate the model through simulations and apply it to real-world data to illustrate its efficacy.

This research introduces a dynamic framework for multigroup societies addressing both closed (intergenerational mobility) and open (lateral migration) systems. Within this model, each group is characterized by a specific retention and expansion probability, representing the likelihood individuals remain within their current group across generations versus transitioning to another. We demonstrate that, similar to prior findings in parallel static frameworks, opportunities as defined by the likelihood of upward movement are distributed according to a bipartite structure contingent upon how groups are classified. Specifically, social structures exhibiting higher internal homogeneity (where members of one group have a stronger prior affinity to join another than external group members) naturally result in unequal opportunities, creating disparities based on initial group membership. Consequently, a society characterized by strong within-group ties inevitably produces unequal vertical mobility chances. Furthermore, we analyze several multi-group configurations to establish that local two-group interactions do not always predict overall multi-group dynamics. Additionally, while vertical distribution remains the focus, our results indicate that horizontal migration patterns are also influenced by these structural characteristics.

It has been established that, for any consistent quantum system, the link between a particle's spin and its statistical behavior (the spin-statistics connection) holds true in the non-relativistic limit. This finding rests on two key premises: first, that multiple identical particles can occupy various spatial configurations; second, that parity is well-defined. The latter implies possession of intrinsic spin and acts as an involution operator that commutes with all observables. When these conditions are met within any general framework, both possible statistical behaviors arise. This paper demonstrates that if identical particles possess half-integer spin, observing fermionic statistics requires the parity operator to square to either $+1$ or $-1$ (specifically, if the internal parity of the fermions is considered). This specific behavior of paritiy breaks the standard derivation, resulting in no restriction on statistics. The authors subsequently prove that establishing fermionic statistics necessitates the existence of an internal parity operator whose square yields $+1$ for bosons or $-1$ for fermions.

This approach is illustrated through a cooperative game played by multiple agents on a graph, where humans and machines collaboratively construct system models using limited data points and explicit expert structural constraints.

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) operates based on the fundamental quantum principles of uncertainty and no-cloning, granting it inherent resistance to eavesdropping. Although the decoy-state protocol allows for high-rate generation of quantum keys without requiring full phase randomization, it is vulnerable to attacks targeting phases with low uncertainty. In this paper, we demonstrate an effective hacking strategy combined with a counteractive measure: even a eavesdropper unable to perfectly discriminate between decoy and vacuum states can exploit phases with minimal randomization in partially phase-randomized states through standard decoy-state analysis. Decoy-state protocols that omit complete phase randomization, utilizing standard weak coherent pulses with only partial phase randomization, face similar susceptibility once such attacks are established. To mitigate this risk, we propose introducing active phase phasing specifically for pulses exhibiting low uncertainty within the standard QKD framework. Simulation results confirm that this phasing enhances system robustness against our described attack while maintaining fair fairness against eavesdropping.

Recent observations indicate that central galaxies in many galaxy clusters possess shallower surface brightness profiles at peripheries than theoretically predicted, a discrepancy often termed the "core-cusp problem." The prevailing solution involves radio-mode active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback, wherein jets from the central supermassive blackhole inject energy into the intracluster medium (ICM), suppressing AGN accretion and limiting further growth. However, this heating often triggers Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities, causing rising buoyant gas bubbles to fragment and expand as they expand. While fragment expansion is generally assumed to be adiabatic, this study demonstrates that non-adiabatic effects—specifically radiative cooling and thermal conduction—significantly alter bubble dynamics. We utilized the publicly available cosmological zoom-in simulation TNG300-2, which incorporates these physical processes, to analyze bubble behavior. Our results show that including radiative cooling accelerments bubble expansion, whereas thermal conduction tends to slow it down. Crucially, we found that the resulting changes in bubble velocity and expansion rates modify the fragments' shape, causing them to fragment into smaller blobs compared to purely adiabatic scenarios. These findings suggest that realistic physical models, beyond simple adiabatic assumptions, are essential for accurately describing the evolution of bubble clusters in galaxy systems.

This study examines CP violation in the decay systems B→KSπ± and D→KSπ± using proton collision data corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb⁻¹, collected at center-of-mass energies of √s = 7 and 8 TeV by the LHCb detector. The analysis employs the background-dominant decay mode to perform the first direct, model-independent determination of the top quark-like parameter λ for both beauty and charm quark decays, yielding values of (0.074 ± 0.033) for the former and (0.068 ± 0.027) for the latter. These results are consistent with predictions derived from the CKM-matrix framework.

By applying the new bosonic tough strings (NBS) framework, we derive scattering amplitudes for various processes involving closed superstrings, including boson-boson N-gon generation, photon scattering with legs (both even and odd), graviton scattering, photon–photon scattering, and generic interactions between massless strings. These new amplitudes exhibit a rigorous leg symmetry, maintain supergravity-like behavior for their leading terms at low energy, and successfully reduce to the established bosonic string N-gon amplitudes when applied to the massive sector. Based on these findings, we propose a broadened version of Gross's conjecture, which links the amplitudes of different string theories through a shared universal structure.

The advent of next-generation (5G) wireless systems introduces significant challenges in scaling central network management (NRM) due to massive enhancements in data volume, speed, and interconnectivity. While the vision of self-organizing networks (SONs) aims to alleviate this scaling burden through autonomous device operations, the exponential rise in network complexity necessitates that future 5G SNs function as integral components of a robust, large-scale central framework. Consequently, this paper investigates the fundamental shifts required within the 2GPP-defined 2GPP-defined E2 management architecture to support this hybrid model of central support and device autonomy. It outlines the essential characteristics of this future NRM structure, examines current 2GPP standardization progress, and highlights critical research priorities needed for forthcoming 2GPP specifications.

This study introduces a novel transcript formatting strategy for neural audio synthesis that leverages perceptual information. The approach segments transcripts using unit networks, a method designed to capture both phonetic details and fine-grained auditory units. The resulting transcripts are then utilized by text-to-uni-forms (TTS) models. The approach is validated through WER evaluations on the LID-22 dataset and F-2 scores on the LID-22 dataset. The results indicate that using units in this manner improves synthesis performance.

Motion planning is a critical area within mobile robotics, and this paper introduces a data-driven method to enhance existing motion-planning algorithms. We begin by formulating motion planning as multi-stage combined convex programming, utilizing system data to refine the solving process. Specifically, we apply data-driven techniques to construct tighter McCormick envelope relaxations for the nonlinear constraints in the cost function. These relaxed problems generate lower bounds that accelerate the Conex Algorithm by reducing the gap between iterates. We evaluate our approach against standard Conex Algorithm iterations and the heuristic RRT*, with results demonstrating that our method outperforms both benchmarks.

This paper investigates the feasibility of converting one single-particle density matrix into another via completely positive trace-preserving maps. We demonstrate that such transformations are constrained not only by standard majorization conditions but also by stricter limits imposed by specific eigenvalue multiplicities. These findings are equivalent to asserting that completely positive trace-preserving operations are not stochastic under mixing for singlet states. The results extend to mixed states, where the rules for state conversion involve a new construct: the convexly summed sequence of two density matrices, denoted as $\oplus_c$. Our contributions broaden the existing framework established by Boykin et al. [男孩] and finally allow for a complete characterization of state conversion using operator theory.

This work introduces a fully mechanized model of a pendulum that mimics the well-known "sloshing in coffee" phenomenon, originally observed by G. G. Stokes. While the classic effect was studied using a hand-suspended, partially filled flexible pendulum, our fully automated version employs a rigid structure enclosed in a flexible container. Our research details both the physical mechanism and the corresponding mathematical formulation, analyzing the system's dynamics through phase portraits, Poincaré maps, and bifurcation diagrams. We further evaluate the solution using Lyapunov exponents and dimension calculations to understand the attractor's nature. Finally, our findings are contrasted with those derived from a manually controlled pendulum by G. G. Stokes.

In the realm of machine learning, the robust generalization of teaching models is frequently hindered by shifts in data distributions during deployment, a challenge known as distribution shift. To address this, researchers have introduced the Min-Max formulation for the one-stage robust learning problem, which seeks a "min-max value" representing the worst-case generalization error under unknown input distribution variations. Decentralized applications frequently lack global access to aggregate data, necessitating specialized algorithms. This paper introduces DR-DSGD, a decentralized min-max optimization algorithm designed for non-convex objectives coupled with non-stationary step-sizes to tackle robust learning in decentralized contexts. Theoretical analysis confirms that DR-DSGD converges in the limit to the robust min-max value, with an expected convergence rate for non-convex objectives of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}})$. Furthermore, numerical experiments validate these theoretical findings and demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms competing approaches in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

We introduce and investigate the concept of a "hydro puller," defined as an asymmetrically charged object that generates significant force resistance against the fluid in which it moves. These entities are ubiquitous in various heavy-ion collision frameworks, encompassing quasinormal modes of R-charged black holes, acoustic vortices within an AdS-Schwarzschild background, and both free and bound particles inside a hydrophobic medium. By leveraging the work performed as these agents traverse the medium, we propose a mechanism for particle creation and generation during collisions. This study further demonstrates the critical role of "initial state vitality"—a metric reflecting the viscous nature of a system's onset—in explaining experimentally observed transverse momentum distributions of produced particles.

While high-velocity jets are a common feature of young stellar objects, low-velocity outflows are also observed around protostars. This study investigates the origins of these slow outflows by analyzing the L1551 region, which is known for a high-speed jet projected perpendicular to a widespread low-velocity structure. Using position-dependent line broadening in CH₃OH, CH₃CN, and CH₃COOH, the source was resolved into a central point source and a jet component, plus an extended component located 0.1 pc away in the plane of the low-velocity outflow. The spatial scale of this extended structure is estimated at approximately 0.0004 pc. Further, the low-velocity flow is interpreted as a jet that has decelerated after colliding with the massive material of the larger extended structure. Consequently, these findings suggest that even high-speed protostellar jets can help generate or drive low-velocity outflows.

Recent advances in Model Predictive Control (MPC) have introduced an innovative mechanism to balance constrained nonlinear system performance with their operational limits by utilizing an equilibration law that dynamically adjusts the penalty on violations versus performance. While highly effective, this approach demands rigorous proof of feasibility—ensuring that at least one solution exists at every sampling instant—and can struggle with performance during the transient phase before equilibration is reached. This study presents a novel scheme that offers a computationally lighter alternative by fully decoupling feasibility from the equilibration process, thereby eliminating the need for iterative penalty tuning. Instead, it employs a single parameter to govern how constrained nonlinear systems respond to violations. Equilibration is realized through a single optimization problem, and the appropriate value for this parameter is determined offline via a performance-bound analysis of the resulting trajectory.

Planetary bodies experience gravitational attractions from the Sun and receive solar radiation pressure, the latter being slightly weaker. These forces generate eccentricity and inclination variations within planets, categorized as either fully secular or semi-seculer based on the ratio of their oscillation periods to that of the Sun. In fully secular cases, this ratio approaches zero; in semi-seculer cases, it converges to integer values. Under semi-seculer conditions, planar orbital elements undergo periodic fluctuations, whereas the spatial orientation exhibits long-term drifts accompanied by short-term perturbations. This research examines the transition between these two regimes by analyzing the boundaries of the parameter space where semi-seculer resonances emerge. We derive analytical conditions for these resonance boundaries and corroborate them with a numerical study. Employing a Taylor series expansion of the Delaunay Hamiltonian up to the third order, the resonance limits are approximated as quadratic equations involving first- and second-order mean spherical harmonics of the body's shape, alongside trigonometric functions of its orbital elements. Numerically, these boundaries were mapped using the averaging method and the minimum semi-decuration derivative method. The study focuses specifically on Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

The study concludes that this selection offers a consistent and reliable method for simulating optical properties in ab initio-based tight-binding simulations.

In standard Cauchy distribution scenarios, constructing confidence intervals for the location and scale parameters typically relies on the fact that the ratio of two independent standard Cauchy variables follows a $t_3$ distribution. However, when these confidence intervals for the model parameters are required for samples of Cauchy distributions that have not been verified or confirmed beforehand, the initial step involves determining if the data truly fits the standard Cauchy framework. Consequently, this paper introduces a novel approach by leveraging the equivalence between set inclusion tests and score-based hypothesis tests. Specifically, we propose a method to generate confidence intervals for the location and scale parameters of unverified Cauchy distributions.

Basket trials represent an emerging clinical trial format intended to assess individual treatments across multiple patient subgroups simultaneously. By sharing information between these subgroups, precise treatment effect estimates can be obtained with smaller sample sizes. However, standard analyses often struggle to specify the extent to which data borrowing occurs. This study introduces a Bayesian framework for sample size calculation in basket trials that allows flexible, subgroup-specific borrowing of information. The approach utilizes reparameterization to isolate the true treatment effect from the data-sharing level. Posterior distributions for this isolated effect are then derived through Markov chain Monte Carlo (MMC) simulations, which inform the required sample size to achieve a target precision. Model parameters are estimated via cross-validation to enhance accuracy, and the methodology's validity is confirmed through simulations alongside a practical application.

The industrial sector increasingly demands precision industrial systems with higher throughput, driving a need for sub-nanometer tracking accuracy alongside high-speed movements exceeding 1 m/s. Achieving these figures using standard linear stages is often prohibitively expensive; consequently, affordable linear positioning systems with equivalent performance are required. One approach involves Linear and Polymeric Scaling (LPV) Control, which adapts controlled-synthesis control theory by parameterizing system dynamics based on a specific variable, such as actuator velocity. Pre-trained models (which we refer to as the source) are becoming increasingly popular due to their vast parameter counts and superior performance. However, their massive size hinders their use in many practical scenarios. Knowledge Distillation (KD) offers a solution by compressing these sources into smaller, more deployable student models. Unsupervised Logits Aggregation (ILA) is an existing KD strategy that requires no auxiliary data; yet, it often yields suboptimal results because it treats all teacher outputs uniformly. Our approach, called Pairwise ILA (PILE), introduces teacher weighting to improve aggregation. PILE iteratively refines how a student learns from multiple teachers by focusing on pairwise interactions. In each iteration, it calculates dynamic importance scores for teachers based on their unique knowledge contributions relative to others, aggregating logits using this refined perspective. Crucially, PILE computes these weights through pure model comparison, avoiding the need for external references or ground truth data. Experiments demonstrate that PILE significantly boosts the area under the Precision-Recall curve compared to ILA and achieves competitive performance with data-driven methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/rohitgarg10/PAIRWISE_ILA.

The search for ultralight dark matter (ULDM) has become a prominent area within contemporary physics, as such hypothetical particles could exist as new elementary forms. This study presents an enhanced experimental setup at the B2C (B2 Coupler) structure of the Spallation Neutron Source (SNs) at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL), designed to detect ULDM signals. The instrument operates on a resonance principle where the coupling between two pendulums, affected by a hypothetical ultralight matter field, creates measurable strength variations. This method offers distinct advantages over traditional acceleration-based approaches, including greater sensitivity to very low force variations and reduced background noise. This novel framework enables a more rigorous evaluation of the B2C configuration's capabilities in seeking ultralight matter, specifically targeting frequency ranges from 0.1 to 100 Hz with a sensitivity threshold between 10$^{-23}$ and 10$^{-25}$ m/s$^{2}$. This strategy holds promise for detecting dark matter in the mass spectrum spanning roughly $10^{-7}$ to $10^{-2}$ eV/c$^{2}$, corresponding to ultralight bosonic particles. The study further details the experimental progress achieved to date.
